Interviewer:	I’ll tell you a bit about what we’re doing to begin with then. The project is looking at engineering students, but we’ve decided to include design technology students in that 

Subject:	Ok.

Interviewer:	Partly because I think your course includes quite a bit of engineering and because we’re looking at engineering as a male dominated industry (mm) because design technology is as well. Are you going on a placement?

Subject:	I’m intending to.

Interviewer:	Yeah. We’re mainly interviewing placement students because we would like to go and interview them again, while they’re on placement and what we’re trying to do is find out people’s expectations about the placement and then see…

Subject:	How it turns out.

Interviewer:	Yeah, but we’re also interested the reasons as well that you chose to go into this field and experiences of the course so far and things like that. At the end of it all we’re going to put together a guidance document, which we’re going to give to the engineering councils and bodies, and hopefully improve the situation for women in the industry. I’ll start off by asking some background questions about why you wanted to do design & technology and things like that. What ‘A’ levels did you do?

Subject:	I did a strange mix. English combined, design technology, physics and general studies.

Interviewer:	Ok.

Subject:	And I did an ‘AS’ in Art.

Interviewer:	OK, and what type of school did you go to?

Subject:	Grammar School.

Interviewer:	Was it a girls’ school or?

Subject:	It was girls only, up till sixth form and then we amalgamated with the boys’ Grammar next door.

Interviewer:	Ok, have you got any previous work experience in the industry?

Subject:	I’ve done work experience at GCSE and at lower sixth as well, in – the first one was architecture but the second was more to do with the [company] sports cars, in [town]. So that was cool.

Interviewer:	Ok what do your parents do? Are either of them in the industry?

Subject:	No, my mum is currently at university – she gave up a job at a university, and decided to go back and study. So mum’s doing International Business at the moment, and my dad is self employed and basically does a bit of everything at the moment.

Interviewer:	OK then, when and why do you think that you decided to do design & technology?

Subject:	Probably first year – first year of secondary school. Year 7, because the teachers were nice to me. The teachers were nice and it was a cool place to go and there wasn’t much else to do at lunchtimes, so you could go there and just do whatever you wanted to and it builds your confidence, with the machinery and everything. And it just seemed to be something I was OK at but I understood the mechanics and the physics of it as well – so I just tied the two together.

Interviewer:	OK have your family been supportive of what you want to do?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	OK 

Subject:	There’s been lots of views, if you want to know, but mum’s very proud of me and because I’m a girl doing a man’s job type of thing. My dad tends to steer clear of the issue a bit because mum and dad are divorced, but my dad’s still very much I can do the DIY, I don’t need any help but my granddad, who is a traditionalist – but he’s exceptionally proud of me. And when I was little he used to encourage me to bang hammer and nails and stuff together so, he’s happy.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think their views have sort of encouraged you really then?

Subject:	Partly yes, but partly because – the reason – there was like a big group of us, all my friends did DT as well because it because it was compulsory then. And I chose it at GCSE because I didn’t like IT and at ‘A’ levels – I got my highest GCSE in DT and ‘cos I chose my ‘A’ levels through my highest subjects at GCSE, because I loved science but at the same time I liked English and the arts as well and if I did science all day I’d get bored, if I did art all day I’d get bored, so DT’s a nice crossover.

Interviewer:	Did you have much careers advice, when you were at school?

Subject:	Lots – they tried to persuade me against it.

Interviewer:	Did they?

Subject:	They really did.

Interviewer:	What did they say to you?

Subject:	They said that I had a good er I would say RSA qualification and I had good communication skills and I got an A at ‘A’ levels in my English, so I should do journalism or management and work in an office environment but I just didn’t want to do that. It’s not me at all because I’ve always got on better with lads really than girls. Still do but erm lads are very straightforward and a spade’s a spade basically. I’d rather have people being honest – I hate having a bit of back stabbing, so I decided to carry on with it because I felt comfortable with it.

Interviewer:	What did the careers people say when you told them what you wanted to get into?

Subject:	They advised me that only a few universities were well known for it and there were only 12 in the country that do industrial design technology and [this university] is the top one, for that and the second is Hull and the rest really don’t feature on the map. So I was told if I wanted to do it then I should go to [this university] and I applied to go to [this university], otherwise it just wasn’t worth it because I wouldn’t get the high enough job at the end of it all.

Interviewer:	So you probably got on better with boys, that’s probably quite interesting considering you went to a girls’ school.

Subject:	Hmm, yeah. I think it’s ‘cos I went to a girls’ school. It just – I don’t know but it’s just the particular people I’ve mixed with but the girls at school were always, she says wearing bright pink, we always very girly, girly and everything revolved around lads and what the lads thought, what the lads did and they were scared of breaking a nail and going on the bandsaw and things like that and it just really annoyed me, because there was a lot of stereotypical – stereotyping rather, at school and it was the lads who did woodwork ‘cos we were still aware of the boys school, even though we weren’t to – like the whole school together. And it’s the boys who did woodwork and the girls who did cookery, ‘cos it’s a traditional school, so we had cookery baskets, which was quite humiliating. But I was trying to prove a point I think by doing that and then – I got ridiculed a lot for it, by the lads at first. And then when you realise you’ve just got to get on with it anyway, they just leave you be.

Interviewer:	OK, that’s interesting that you said that your school was quite stereotyped because some people I’ve spoken to that have been to girls’ schools think that they were maybe encouraged to do the so-called masculine subjects because it was a girls school?

Subject:	It’s varies between places and the different teachers, and the headship changed several times so the view was very different. When I first started there I had a female head teacher, Miss [name], she was wonderful – really girl power. And basically right the way through it was drilled into us that what you think is good, isn’t good enough and that whatever the boys can do you can do 10 times better and if a boy gets an A for something, you’ll only get a B because you could have done better anyway. So there was that real kind of you can do better than the boys all the way through, which she built up my confidence a bit – and that girls don’t need to be housewives and things like that. But at the same time they were still teaching us cookery. So it was a bit of a contradiction to keep the governors happy I think. But then, once I got into sixth form, the girls’ sixth form physically moved over onto the boys’ site so it’s very much lads’ territory, surrounded by lads from first year to final GCSE and then all the sixth form as well, so it was only 2 years worth of girls whereas it lower sixth and upper sixth on the site, so they was like ooh, it’s a girl, walking down the corridor, but – I don’t know the boys got encouraged in sports and the girls got encouraged in communication and presentation skills. But as long as you did well, they kept off your back basically.

Interviewer:	Did you do much research career wise?

Subject:	Lots and lots and lots because I’d got a couple of friends who were 4 or 5 years older, from school because at school I was involved in music a lot. So I thought it was a really good opportunity to build up my confidence and mix with the lads at the same time, but get to know people who were a bit older, because I always seemed to be a bit older than my year – I was always seemed to get on better with a bit – people who were a bit older than me and er one of the girls had done industrial design technology and had come out and found a really, really good job and she was a car designer now – it was wonderful but then I was aware that the people who did management, or journalism didn’t have jobs to go to. And, even though the careers advisor was wonderful, at school, and she was saying oh you know, it’s a good steady job and it’s been around for years so it’ll be around for many more years – industrial design’s always been a bit of a hazy one and – because we can fit into lots of different roles like design engineers, or car designers or graphic designers and even on the university campus here, if people ask you what you do – you say industrial design technology, they’re like ‘oh, that’s nice’ (‘what is it?’) Yeah, and er most of them tend to think it’s all Art Schooly BA but it’s not because we do a BSc and we have to do number crunchers like everybody else.

Interviewer:	I was surprised that it was in the Social Sciences faculty, and not in engineering.

Subject:	Yeah, and that’s a problem in the university, between the students. Because – because I’m doing a BSc, some of the students who I have modules with – engineering like mech eng. Manufacturing engineers are like oh, and there is that definite you’re not doing an Eng. So you don’t know what you’re talking about really but stuff ‘em. We don’t know anything.

Interviewer:	Did you always want to do the sandwich course?

Subject:	No. At first I thought erm I wanted a career – I knew that I had to go to University, ‘cos I was like had to work hard – I’ve had all these things drummed into me, you have to work hard, to get to University, to get to the career, and at first I didn’t want to come to university because it was – I’m no longer a child and I was away from home and oh, it’s a bit scary. And then once I got my head round that, and it was 4 hours away from home and – I don’t know really, it’s – my confidence has grown since I’ve been here but I know there are so many fields of design technology I want to make sure I aim and find it, because you can narrow down your modules and be very specific about what you want to do and I want to make sure I’m going into the right area for me. Otherwise someone’s gonna swipe a job off me, so – and seeing placement basically as a taster and to try and work out – even if I hate what I do for a year, at least I can rule that out and say right, you know I’ve only got 40 odd more fields to cover now. But that’s why basically – and to earn a bit, as well.

Interviewer:	OK, Did it ever bother you then that the industry was so male dominated?

Subject:	Mm no, because I think it always has been. Because right the way through school, there’s always been a hint of attitude along the way, especially in the department here, there is a definitely male/female thing going on and I don’t know. At school, like as in [name] the Girls Grammar school, the male DT teacher has always treated us as if we were lads basically and it was like oh why the heck are you crying, get on with it, a bit of dust – it’s like dust and dirt in the gut it’ll do it good and it – you know, you don’t need a tetanus shot and things like that, but then at sixth form, I think the teachers weren’t used to teaching girls – I was the only girl in my DT class, and it was like oooh, is she gonna cry? Oh no. They were very, very gentle with me. But here, it’s – some of the teachers are very – get on with it – I don’t care if you’re a girl, just get on with it, which is fine by me but some of them are like ‘are you alright mate?’ to the lads and they say ‘oh are you alright lovey, are you OK?’ And it’s like ‘yes, cheers lovey I am’. And it’s just – that annoys me a bit. But you get it anywhere though because if you go into somewhere like [shop] or something, if you need supplies for your project, and you go in with a group of lads then with the group of lads and it’s like Oh are you alright mate? What you looking for? And then they’ll come and coax you round the shop and try and explain to you what everything is. And I go, oh yes that’s such and such a thing, you know – they don’t like that they go ah, you’re a girl and you know, which I don’t know – it amuses me. I try not to get annoyed about it, take the mickey out of them, but…

Interviewer:	Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do design technology?

Subject:	No, cos they’d take all my jobs. Er, yes, definitely, but I think it is gradually coming through. However, I was aware at primary school – because I went to a normal everyday primary school, and even though, obviously, it wasn’t design and technology to the extent of machinery, but resources were very, very thin on the ground, so I think if I’d been to another school and this isn’t being ‘schoolist’ but if I’d been to another school, then I don’t think the resources would’ve been as good, but mine had lots and lots of bandsaws, there was lots and lots of machinery and better facilities, to be honest than the department here and newer machines and they worked properly and they don’t break and properly trained how to use them, rather than just get along with it – you were treated like an adult and so things like bandsaw blades – if one breaks in the department, it’s the end of the world, and a technician gets all kitted out and it’s a big deal for him to repair this big saw and everything, but back at ‘A’ level it was a case of if you broke it, there’s a new blade, go and do it. And you used to do it, so we are a bit cushioned – but it’s OK.

Interviewer:	OK, What do you think needs to be done to encourage more women into the career?

Subject:	Throw a ball. I think it’s not anything really to do with the women it’s more to do with the men and try and educate them a bit because there are lads on my course – not all of them, but if a girl starts up a machine or anything, it’s like oooh, and they stand there watching, waiting for you to break something or it’s kind of Oh, are you OK? Let me help you. Well why, it’s my project get off, you know, you’ll ruin it. But there’s definitely that kind of – I don’t know, barrier in a way. Some guys are absolutely fine and they’re just – let you get on with it and treat you like close friends, just let you get on with it and if anything asks for help because you’re more accurate than they are and you can fit your hand into smaller places, so you can do more detailed work in electronics. But most of them do have a very ooooooh, it’s a girl – so I think it needs to be made acceptable to them. But even if it was it wouldn’t come through for generations because it’s how – it’s like parents influence and everything going down.

Interviewer:	Do you think that women are aware enough about what is actually involved, to be able to make a decision whether to choose the subject or not?

Subject:	No, because I don’t think the – even though the subject itself’s been around for donkeys years and in – actually in major industry – manufacturing industry, it’s just as well known as engineering, but because a lot of the modules can only be dealt with at university level onwards, in-depth, then people don’t have any idea as to what it is beforehand. Because the thing about engineering – oh, engineering, lots of sums and if it’s automotive it’s to do with cars and if it’s you know, aeronautical, it’s to do with planes – and that’s simple enough, but industrial design technology is like ooh, what is it? And there’s – people just don’t know and I just describe it outside as probe design into physics and there’s so much more – there’s like ergonomics and there’s everything and I love certain modules, but, to the outside world it’s like why? Why are you doing that? What’s the point to that? It’s like well it links in with this, and this, and this and then it’s like, so?

Interviewer:	They don’t realise what an impact it has?

Subject:	No, because a good example is, I went to the Canary Islands on holiday, at Easter, with my boyfriend. And there was like a chair in front of me, like a normal patio chair but it was really, really intricately designed. So something like that can’t be mass produced, it has to be like a one off but the machine would’ve cost a hell of a lot, so that’s why oh, I’m looking at it, trying to work out if it’s injection mould or cast mould or something like – and my boyfriend’s like, what on earth are you doing? And I’m like oh, oh, I wonder – and it’s just once you know about processes and things, you start picking stuff up in – I used to think my DT teacher was a complete nutcase but you do start to pick stuff up and look at it, and I don’t take things for granted anymore. But there’s lots of politics and legislation and things involved as well and it’s not just a case of go away and draw a pretty picture and make it – which I think a lot of people think it is. It’s all kind of like, well, this directive’s come in and you can only use x grams of polymer and things like that. It’s tricky, but if industrial design wasn’t around, a hell of a lot of people would notice it – ‘cos they wouldn’t have anything to sit on mainly! Things like that.

Interviewer:	OK, what characteristics do you think make a good designer?

Subject:	Ooh, do I have to have them?

Interviewer:	No more like an ideal.

Subject:	An ideal – communication skills definitely, from sourcing out needs and wants, to presenting the ideas and communicating with manufacturers and things, because even now, having to ring up manufacturers and things and say, how do you make this? How do you make that? And then the lads are saying well, they won’t tell me, but they’ll tell me and so I use it to my advantage then, but…

Interviewer:	That was one of my next questions.

Subject:	Erm, so communication, confidence – definitely, to design something and within the DT department it’s a harsh world, to design something and stand by it all the way through, and even have the lecturers going hmm, ok that’s a bit different – so I’m not conformist, not at all that’s boring. And er, to be able to stand by it – even if it falls flat on its face – to still say, well, you know, it’s obviously the world’s not ready for it quite yet and just to pull yourself together. Erm, a love of sleep deprivation (laughter) and to put your work first – definitely – because my life is DT, and that’s really sad, but it is and everything else, apart from family, comes second. And even family – well, you know, if you’ve got a major project, then who knows? But erm…I don’t know – a good sense of humour. If things go wrong you need to be able to laugh about it, and to get on with people as well. And you have to be quite adaptable as to who you get on with even if people are annoying the hell out of you. You’ve still got to be OK with them, because you’re gonna see them everyday, just like in the workplace – you’ve got to er – if people get stressed out, as they do, and tetchy and things go wrong, and they start snapping at you – you’ve just got to take it on the chin and leave them be. 

Interviewer:	Yeah – do you have to do a lot of group work?

Subject:	Yeah. I hate it – I really hate group work because I always end up being a leader, which is my fifth one, being good at leadership – you sometimes have to take over – and I don’t like it because I always end up doing more work, but I can’t stand people dawdling. It really, really annoys me. And like ooh well, and I would say it’s mainly the girls – not all of them but there’s a certain section of girls, who hang together, who dither. And it’s not their personality, it’s just the way girls are I think. I mean they always ask the lads for opinions before they do things.

Interviewer:	Like they don’t have confidence in their own work?

Subject:	Exactly. And it’s – why not – why can’t they be so confident and you’re completely, you know, wiping the slate clean again – I have to build it up again, but they’re oh, what do you think? Oh I don’t know. Did you watch Neighbours? And it’s like they really let the side down – they really, really do. So you need to have the guts to – it’s all about guts really. You just need to stand up there and say right, this needs to be done. You’re gonna do it and you’re gonna do and it’s just like, deal with it, basically.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that there are advantages to doing group work though?

Subject:	Mm, yes, yes because you learn, at school, there are advantages to group work but in practice no, I hate group work. I like group work, in the fact that it gives me – I feel personally responsible for my own work because I’m guaranteed to do – to the absolutely best capability that I can do. If it’s just me, you know, I’ll leave bits that I really shouldn’t do but it’s OK. I know the difference between – you know – like a 40% OK if I’m tired, like and 70% group work. So I tend to put more effort in because I don’t want to be the one that brings the group down, but at the same time it’s usually me saying right then, so I seem to be always the one that’s trying to enthuse everybody and I don’t like that.

Interviewer:	Do you think the fact that you have done so much group work, do you think that will help you when you go into the industry?

Subject:	I think it’s actually making me less tolerant of people. As I’m going along I seem to be stuck with problem people, because right the way through since starting I’ve always been classified as the ‘good girl’ that would put people on the straight and narrow and there’s always a naughty boy sitting with me at my table, at primary school, so I could have this wonderful, angelic effect on them. But erm, I don’t know, it’s – I think it’s the way that people handle pressure that’s the big crunch for when it comes to group work, in DT because I’ll be – I feel it, blooming heck I feel it, and I don’t have much sleep and sometimes I burst into tears for no reason, but not when there are lads around. And er, it’s just – for group work it’s just like I’m like the face on it, it’s kind of like you know, we can do this and positive talk and I talk myself out of it. But, if I’m put with people who are ‘oohh, how many pages did you do?’ And ‘what colour’s your folio?’ And yes, they do go that low – then I’m like who cares? You know. And it’s like ‘well I’ve done 60 pages’ and it’s like ‘oooh’. And yet they’ll have somebody really like kind of ‘what type font – space are you using? What size font are you using?’ And it’s stupid – it really is. That’s when the group work really irritates me – it’s people discussing little, tiny things instead of doing the work, and they always get distracted. And if there’s a lad he’s like, oh did you watch the rugby last night? Oh you going to [student union event]? And if it’s a girl it’s like, oh did you watch Neighbours? Oh what did you think? Ooh, what’s gonna happen? Oh I’m so stressed out, my boyfriend says this and it’s like, I just don’t talk about my boyfriend in DT at all. Like with a couple of close friends in DT, I did – admittedly, but if there’s group work to do, I do the group work because I don’t want to do in the evening – my free time is when I want to spend time with my boyfriend. I’ve just finished a bad group work project, so that’s not a good question right now.

Interviewer:	OK, going back to the characteristics – do you think that any of the characteristics are more male or female characteristics?

Subject:	No, because, this is my mum’s upbringing now – this is dreadful – I sound like my mum, but – I’ll have to explain my family history - my mum and dad got divorced when I was 5, my mum suddenly became very feminist and she said you can do anything, don’t end up like your dad and so I’ve always had it drummed into me, confidence and things like that. But I don’t think that any characteristic has to be necessarily female or male.

Interviewer:	Do you think that other people probably perceive that it is and that’s why there aren’t so many women in the industry?

Subject:	It’s something that I think – sometimes I feel like a fly on the wall, because sometimes I think the lads forget I’m a girl. Like oh, phew, oh and things like that and it’s like OK, fair enough. And I think, to be honest, because I’ve been with my boyfriend now for a year and a half, if I was single – like completely single – then I think I’d be viewed slightly differently, but I think I’m – being just safe at the moment and allowed into that group because I’m not going to go oooh and start giggling in a corner, but – some of the lads – like last year were definitely surprised that girls were doing things and that girls were confident, because I don’t have problems with presentations and like – some people, male and female, like presentations, some despise them and start shaking and passing out and stuff and last year we did a big presentation and my partner was the tallest, big captain of the rugby team - really tough, popular guy and he was lovely – he was a real softie but he actually fainted, in the middle of the presentation, and I was just there talking away because I imagined my mum sat at the top, near the exit sign, and just concentrate on her, type of thing. But I think that’s just schooling as well just the way you’re taught things and I just heard umph, and he was there on the floor and he’s still getting ridiculed for it, but if it was a girl I don’t think she would be ridiculed. But because it wasn’t expected from him, but, there’s a lot of preconceptions, a lot of people are like, oh you do woodwork, oh – and they always look at my nails, which aren’t bad – still got spray paint on some of them but – ‘oooh, and your nails are quite long. Tell me do you wear pink? And there does seem to be this preconception if you do engineering or a science degree or whatever then you’re a butch lesbian basically and that really irritates me – because I’m not, you know. I’m bubbly and I’m happy and I’m just – not that butch lesbians can’t be bubbly and happy, but you know? I don’t think that sexuality has anything to do with capabilities.

Interviewer:	Yeah, but there’s this perception that women and engineery type things don’t go together and if they do you can’t be feminine?

Subject:	But some of the things the lads in DT come out with and they forget that I’m there, they’re all like oooh, all girls who do engineering oh they’re all plain and they’re all boring. It’s like all girls who do DT oh they’re either super duper arty or just you know, keep themselves to themselves. And it’s like well, where do I fit in to all of this? You know – oh well, they kind of have that look on their face like to say Katie was here, damn.

Interviewer:	Do you think that about the other girls though sometimes?

Subject:	Definitely – definitely. I don’t know there’s – everyone’s got the right to dress, to act whether – do what you need as long as it doesn’t do harm to another what I believe in basically – but some of them, they’re just like mullet hair – mullet hair styles – girls with mullets, for God’s sake why? And they’re walking round looking like they’ve been attacked by a strimmer with you know like eye shadow – like eye shadow going and over the eyebrows and everything – that’s – they look like they’re in the middle of a Vivienne Westwood fashion show and stiletto heels, in the department when you’ve got to walk between – it’s just not practical, and I think what are you doing? But some of the lads to be honest, some of the lads are very, very preened and if they got their hands dirty – you know – well, it would kill them and they all wear perfect hair, but the lads is just as stereotypical as the girls. Definitely, because they all fit into either surfer, or arty or Mr Popular lad who’s always been in the sports team – a bit of a player and then there’s the quiet ones and I’ve got a problem with the sporty ones because they’re very, very arrogant and it’s their confidence – girls are – because I can put my work up on the wall and say oh yeah, and all my mates are like oh yeah its really good, and I’m thinking you’re only saying that because you’re my friend, thanks but – and you say it back to them – but think hmm. And then, a lad’ll come along and say that’s rubbish. You could do better than that and it’s – but at least it’s an honest opinion. And it’s – I don’t know – it’s – then you get lads coming in, and it is the lads to be fair – the big, tall lads especially, who are put up the work and they sit there and go yeah, look at that. And they’ve just – they’re loving themselves completely, and I can sit there and smile and think, yeah, that’s OK, inside I’m thinking I should have done this, I should have done that – Oh God, she’s done that too (Sharp intake of breath) you know, and it’s a face worse than death if they’ve got the same coloured mount board and other worries like that. But then some of them just sit there and go yeah – you know, they’re just smoothing out their T-shirts and things and that’s – oh, that annoys me. It’s one thing being confident but it’s another thing when, you know, they’re walking about – yeah. I think the best invention would be kind of like a headband with a mirror in front so they’re permanently surrounded by beauty – it’s just – and they are bitchy. And some of the lads are worse than the girls, about everybody in general and it tends to be the lads who slag off the teachers, rather than the girls. I think that’s kind of a male struggle and like sons and fathers – who takes the power and things like that. But there’s lots of very heated arguments and it’s all to do with – well, I think they’re pissing up trees – they’re marking out territory. In a department like that where you can have a little workspace – like lots and lots of – I don’t know whether you’ve been in there or not? (No) Lots and lots of big work benches and you go in and you junk your stuff, you do your work, go out, come back after lunch, you come in, you have to work round whatever with dreaded freshers or finalists – which are a bit scary – and you just have to get on with it. And then, in lectures anybody sits with anybody basically – ‘cos of all the group work we all know, like somebody’s worked somebody, so therefore they must be OK. But then the big groups come in and they have to sit together, even if there’s like 2 spaces and there’ll be 6 lads, and it’s all the preening lads, have to stay in that one tiny space standing in the model of this little circle because they just can’t be separated. And things like with – it comes even as low as David Beckham, with Victoria and how the press are gunning in on all the controversy and everything, but no-one’s actually seen the fact that this woman here is – it’s awful, even for it to be suggested – I haven’t seen even one report that’s even slightly seen it from her point of view.

Interviewer:	No, everything’s just slagging her off. How does she still be parading in public?

Subject:	Yeah, and how she left him and that’s probably with my family background, and my mum and dad, and the fact that my dad is an older, fatter, David Beckham. In fact much older and fatter, and with a lot less hair but I don’t think that women are given equal rights within publicity and in politics, even though they’re supposed to be. The women that seem to be high profiled in politics are – and I can’t remember her blooming name now – Anne Widdacombe, big battle axes and they’re not – you don’t see any young or pre – I’m not saying that women are hardly ever pretty, but you don’t see any young, pretty women getting out there and really doing anything or they are but it’s just not being talked about. Because – especially, Government in a way is a bit like DT there’s a lot of old establishment – the old boys who went to the old polytechnics and things and they all went to – you know – they were all together and they remember the good old days, and there’s a woman ooooh and I think people are to eager to please them – to conform, because nothing ever changes if you conform all the time. I’m not saying have a complete female outburst but things in industry will only change if women get high profiled in the media and politics, because within media, like the most – I’m trying to think of who I can think of in the media in the last couple of years is things like Louise Woodward, things like that. Women don’t seem to be publicised for – it’s like the fact that she was female and she was a nanny – very female role – and so that she didn’t fulfil accordingly, to the story – didn’t fulfil her female, nanny, maternal role or like erm sexual harassment cases all over the place. And that only – that seems to get more coverage than like you know, this is the girl that came up from nothing and now she’s doing this and it’s all about how women seem to be tripping up. If Beckham scores a goal, it’s all over the front pages. You know good old Johnny Wilkinson – I mean I understand, but still it’s all over the entire place. But it’s like women’s football, women’s rugby, stuff like that, you just don’t hear about that at all, and I think that’s probably because there were men high up within the media as well, like the media hierarchy, rather than the women. So I think it’s just – it’s a gradual process I think it’s going to take many, many, many, many years for it all to slowly start filtering through. But I don’t know – there’s lots of views on it, it’s just it annoys me because you can only get so far before you hit another barrier of people – another row of opinions, and at the minute I’m getting a bit fed up with having to justify myself to people because I am who I am and men are allowed to be tired and stressed out – it doesn’t mean it’s the time of the month, it doesn’t mean that they’re having a bad hair day. Girls in DT have to tie their hair back – bad hair days everyday - and stuff like that – it’s just…and that really annoys – if anything, ever if I’m look down, for whatever reason, like for instance my grandpa died, last year, and I looked down and I went into the department, I thought chin up, I’ve got a deadline, chin up, go in, and my close friends knew and they were a bit – ‘cos you just don’t know how to act and it’s just like treat me blooming normally will you? You’ll make me cry. And then a lad walked past and he was like, oh is it time of the month? And you’re just like – how – what gives him the right to say that personal thing to me. Like I don’t start talking about bodily men’s stuff, you know, it’s like – I could come out with all kinds of things but I won’t do it but I wouldn’t dream of going up to somebody else and saying – like girls joke and we say it to each other, ‘cos you can tell, but the lads don’t have a clue – so, it’s gonna take a long, long, long, long, long time. And, it might happen when it – for instance like my room mate is Dutch and she seems to have a completely different outlook on almost everything in life but she’s doing international business like my mother, so she’s very vocal about politics and rights, and feminism and everything like that. Whether you like it or not, she’ll talk to you about it, and she uses this chat up line (lost words) and she started telling people about feminist rights and I was studying this today and you can see the lads going (sharp intake of breath) feminist lesbian, move out the way - but she’s lovely – she really is lovely but she’s – she doesn’t see any barrier between men and women in industry, or anything, because the world’s an open book to her and in that way I think she’s naïve but she honestly believes that if she believes in herself she can achieve anything, and I think – I agree with that to a certain extent, but there’s always going to be somewhere – a big chairman, somewhere, that got the job because his grandfather’s grandfather has always had the job. He’s gonna be a bit threatened by this woman coming into the engineering industry because – for instance, whenever I go into interviews, I have like this big issue talking about the suits – because I’ve got a trouser suit and nothing against trousers obviously, but personally I would feel – because I have to wear trousers all day, every day for my course – I would feel more comfortable in my skirt suit – only because I’ve grown taller I can’t wear it, because it’s a bit wee but it’s just – I don’t want to see – I feel I would be at a loss if I went into an interview, in a skirt, and that shouldn’t be an issue. I mean if you were a bloke and you went into an interview in a skirt, fair enough you’d be at a loss but it shouldn’t be – I shouldn’t have to dress with big kind of like power shoulder blades – shoulder pads, you know, the big power suit type job, to try and blend in, in a masculine environment. I shouldn’t have to blend in like a bloke. You know, cos I’m there in my own right and if I want my hair down, I’ll have my hair down and stuff like that. I don’t want to – I’m not gonna kick up a stink, but I don’t feel I should hide who I am. Sorry, I’ve rambled for ages.

Interviewer:	No, that’s OK, that’s been really interesting. Thank you very much.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I’ll tell you a bit about what we’re doing to begin with then. The project is looking at engineering students, but we’ve decided to include design technology students in that

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Ok.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Partly because I think your course includes quite a bit of engineering and because we’re looking at engineering as a male dominated industry (mm) because design technology is as well. Are you going on a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’m intending to.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. We’re mainly interviewing placement students because we would like to go and interview them again, while they’re on placement and what we’re trying to do is find out people’s expectations about the placement and then see…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: How it turns out.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, but we’re also interested the reasons as well that you chose to go into this field and experiences of the course so far and things like that. At the end of it all we’re going to put together a guidance document, which we’re going to give to the engineering councils and bodies, and hopefully improve the situation for women in the industry. I’ll start off by asking some background questions about why you wanted to do design & technology and things like that. What ‘A’ levels did you do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I did a strange mix. English combined, design technology, physics and general studies.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: And I did an ‘AS’ in Art.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, and what type of school did you go to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Grammar School.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Was it a girls’ school or?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It was girls only, up till sixth form and then we amalgamated with the boys’ Grammar next door.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, have you got any previous work experience in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’ve done work experience at GCSE and at lower sixth as well, in – the first one was architecture but the second was more to do with the [company] sports cars, in [town]. So that was cool.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok what do your parents do? Are either of them in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, my mum is currently at university – she gave up a job at a university, and decided to go back and study. So mum’s doing International Business at the moment, and my dad is self employed and basically does a bit of everything at the moment.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK then, when and why do you think that you decided to do design & technology?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Probably first year – first year of secondary school. Year 7, because the teachers were nice to me. The teachers were nice and it was a cool place to go and there wasn’t much else to do at lunchtimes, so you could go there and just do whatever you wanted to and it builds your confidence, with the machinery and everything. And it just seemed to be something I was OK at but I understood the mechanics and the physics of it as well – so I just tied the two together.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK have your family been supportive of what you want to do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: There’s been lots of views, if you want to know, but mum’s very proud of me and because I’m a girl doing a man’s job type of thing. My dad tends to steer clear of the issue a bit because mum and dad are divorced, but my dad’s still very much I can do the DIY, I don’t need any help but my granddad, who is a traditionalist – but he’s exceptionally proud of me. And when I was little he used to encourage me to bang hammer and nails and stuff together so, he’s happy.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think their views have sort of encouraged you really then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Partly yes, but partly because – the reason – there was like a big group of us, all my friends did DT as well because it because it was compulsory then. And I chose it at GCSE because I didn’t like IT and at ‘A’ levels – I got my highest GCSE in DT and ‘cos I chose my ‘A’ levels through my highest subjects at GCSE, because I loved science but at the same time I liked English and the arts as well and if I did science all day I’d get bored, if I did art all day I’d get bored, so DT’s a nice crossover.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you have much careers advice, when you were at school?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Lots – they tried to persuade me against it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did they?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: They really did.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What did they say to you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: They said that I had a good er I would say RSA qualification and I had good communication skills and I got an A at ‘A’ levels in my English, so I should do journalism or management and work in an office environment but I just didn’t want to do that. It’s not me at all because I’ve always got on better with lads really than girls. Still do but erm lads are very straightforward and a spade’s a spade basically. I’d rather have people being honest – I hate having a bit of back stabbing, so I decided to carry on with it because I felt comfortable with it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What did the careers people say when you told them what you wanted to get into?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: They advised me that only a few universities were well known for it and there were only 12 in the country that do industrial design technology and [this university] is the top one, for that and the second is Hull and the rest really don’t feature on the map. So I was told if I wanted to do it then I should go to [this university] and I applied to go to [this university], otherwise it just wasn’t worth it because I wouldn’t get the high enough job at the end of it all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you probably got on better with boys, that’s probably quite interesting considering you went to a girls’ school.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm, yeah. I think it’s ‘cos I went to a girls’ school. It just – I don’t know but it’s just the particular people I’ve mixed with but the girls at school were always, she says wearing bright pink, we always very girly, girly and everything revolved around lads and what the lads thought, what the lads did and they were scared of breaking a nail and going on the bandsaw and things like that and it just really annoyed me, because there was a lot of stereotypical – stereotyping rather, at school and it was the lads who did woodwork ‘cos we were still aware of the boys school, even though we weren’t to – like the whole school together. And it’s the boys who did woodwork and the girls who did cookery, ‘cos it’s a traditional school, so we had cookery baskets, which was quite humiliating. But I was trying to prove a point I think by doing that and then – I got ridiculed a lot for it, by the lads at first. And then when you realise you’ve just got to get on with it anyway, they just leave you be.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that’s interesting that you said that your school was quite stereotyped because some people I’ve spoken to that have been to girls’ schools think that they were maybe encouraged to do the so-called masculine subjects because it was a girls school?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s varies between places and the different teachers, and the headship changed several times so the view was very different. When I first started there I had a female head teacher, Miss [name], she was wonderful – really girl power. And basically right the way through it was drilled into us that what you think is good, isn’t good enough and that whatever the boys can do you can do 10 times better and if a boy gets an A for something, you’ll only get a B because you could have done better anyway. So there was that real kind of you can do better than the boys all the way through, which she built up my confidence a bit – and that girls don’t need to be housewives and things like that. But at the same time they were still teaching us cookery. So it was a bit of a contradiction to keep the governors happy I think. But then, once I got into sixth form, the girls’ sixth form physically moved over onto the boys’ site so it’s very much lads’ territory, surrounded by lads from first year to final GCSE and then all the sixth form as well, so it was only 2 years worth of girls whereas it lower sixth and upper sixth on the site, so they was like ooh, it’s a girl, walking down the corridor, but – I don’t know the boys got encouraged in sports and the girls got encouraged in communication and presentation skills. But as long as you did well, they kept off your back basically.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you do much research career wise?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Lots and lots and lots because I’d got a couple of friends who were 4 or 5 years older, from school because at school I was involved in music a lot. So I thought it was a really good opportunity to build up my confidence and mix with the lads at the same time, but get to know people who were a bit older, because I always seemed to be a bit older than my year – I was always seemed to get on better with a bit – people who were a bit older than me and er one of the girls had done industrial design technology and had come out and found a really, really good job and she was a car designer now – it was wonderful but then I was aware that the people who did management, or journalism didn’t have jobs to go to. And, even though the careers advisor was wonderful, at school, and she was saying oh you know, it’s a good steady job and it’s been around for years so it’ll be around for many more years – industrial design’s always been a bit of a hazy one and – because we can fit into lots of different roles like design engineers, or car designers or graphic designers and even on the university campus here, if people ask you what you do – you say industrial design technology, they’re like ‘oh, that’s nice’ (‘what is it?’) Yeah, and er most of them tend to think it’s all Art Schooly BA but it’s not because we do a BSc and we have to do number crunchers like everybody else.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I was surprised that it was in the Social Sciences faculty, and not in engineering.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, and that’s a problem in the university, between the students. Because – because I’m doing a BSc, some of the students who I have modules with – engineering like mech eng. Manufacturing engineers are like oh, and there is that definite you’re not doing an Eng. So you don’t know what you’re talking about really but stuff ‘em. We don’t know anything.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you always want to do the sandwich course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. At first I thought erm I wanted a career – I knew that I had to go to University, ‘cos I was like had to work hard – I’ve had all these things drummed into me, you have to work hard, to get to University, to get to the career, and at first I didn’t want to come to university because it was – I’m no longer a child and I was away from home and oh, it’s a bit scary. And then once I got my head round that, and it was 4 hours away from home and – I don’t know really, it’s – my confidence has grown since I’ve been here but I know there are so many fields of design technology I want to make sure I aim and find it, because you can narrow down your modules and be very specific about what you want to do and I want to make sure I’m going into the right area for me. Otherwise someone’s gonna swipe a job off me, so – and seeing placement basically as a taster and to try and work out – even if I hate what I do for a year, at least I can rule that out and say right, you know I’ve only got 40 odd more fields to cover now. But that’s why basically – and to earn a bit, as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, Did it ever bother you then that the industry was so male dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm no, because I think it always has been. Because right the way through school, there’s always been a hint of attitude along the way, especially in the department here, there is a definitely male/female thing going on and I don’t know. At school, like as in [name] the Girls Grammar school, the male DT teacher has always treated us as if we were lads basically and it was like oh why the heck are you crying, get on with it, a bit of dust – it’s like dust and dirt in the gut it’ll do it good and it – you know, you don’t need a tetanus shot and things like that, but then at sixth form, I think the teachers weren’t used to teaching girls – I was the only girl in my DT class, and it was like oooh, is she gonna cry? Oh no. They were very, very gentle with me. But here, it’s – some of the teachers are very – get on with it – I don’t care if you’re a girl, just get on with it, which is fine by me but some of them are like ‘are you alright mate?’ to the lads and they say ‘oh are you alright lovey, are you OK?’ And it’s like ‘yes, cheers lovey I am’. And it’s just – that annoys me a bit. But you get it anywhere though because if you go into somewhere like [shop] or something, if you need supplies for your project, and you go in with a group of lads then with the group of lads and it’s like Oh are you alright mate? What you looking for? And then they’ll come and coax you round the shop and try and explain to you what everything is. And I go, oh yes that’s such and such a thing, you know – they don’t like that they go ah, you’re a girl and you know, which I don’t know – it amuses me. I try not to get annoyed about it, take the mickey out of them, but…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do design technology?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, cos they’d take all my jobs. Er, yes, definitely, but I think it is gradually coming through. However, I was aware at primary school – because I went to a normal everyday primary school, and even though, obviously, it wasn’t design and technology to the extent of machinery, but resources were very, very thin on the ground, so I think if I’d been to another school and this isn’t being ‘schoolist’ but if I’d been to another school, then I don’t think the resources would’ve been as good, but mine had lots and lots of bandsaws, there was lots and lots of machinery and better facilities, to be honest than the department here and newer machines and they worked properly and they don’t break and properly trained how to use them, rather than just get along with it – you were treated like an adult and so things like bandsaw blades – if one breaks in the department, it’s the end of the world, and a technician gets all kitted out and it’s a big deal for him to repair this big saw and everything, but back at ‘A’ level it was a case of if you broke it, there’s a new blade, go and do it. And you used to do it, so we are a bit cushioned – but it’s OK.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, What do you think needs to be done to encourage more women into the career?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Throw a ball. I think it’s not anything really to do with the women it’s more to do with the men and try and educate them a bit because there are lads on my course – not all of them, but if a girl starts up a machine or anything, it’s like oooh, and they stand there watching, waiting for you to break something or it’s kind of Oh, are you OK? Let me help you. Well why, it’s my project get off, you know, you’ll ruin it. But there’s definitely that kind of – I don’t know, barrier in a way. Some guys are absolutely fine and they’re just – let you get on with it and treat you like close friends, just let you get on with it and if anything asks for help because you’re more accurate than they are and you can fit your hand into smaller places, so you can do more detailed work in electronics. But most of them do have a very ooooooh, it’s a girl – so I think it needs to be made acceptable to them. But even if it was it wouldn’t come through for generations because it’s how – it’s like parents influence and everything going down.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that women are aware enough about what is actually involved, to be able to make a decision whether to choose the subject or not?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, because I don’t think the – even though the subject itself’s been around for donkeys years and in – actually in major industry – manufacturing industry, it’s just as well known as engineering, but because a lot of the modules can only be dealt with at university level onwards, in-depth, then people don’t have any idea as to what it is beforehand. Because the thing about engineering – oh, engineering, lots of sums and if it’s automotive it’s to do with cars and if it’s you know, aeronautical, it’s to do with planes – and that’s simple enough, but industrial design technology is like ooh, what is it? And there’s – people just don’t know and I just describe it outside as probe design into physics and there’s so much more – there’s like ergonomics and there’s everything and I love certain modules, but, to the outside world it’s like why? Why are you doing that? What’s the point to that? It’s like well it links in with this, and this, and this and then it’s like, so?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: They don’t realise what an impact it has?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, because a good example is, I went to the Canary Islands on holiday, at Easter, with my boyfriend. And there was like a chair in front of me, like a normal patio chair but it was really, really intricately designed. So something like that can’t be mass produced, it has to be like a one off but the machine would’ve cost a hell of a lot, so that’s why oh, I’m looking at it, trying to work out if it’s injection mould or cast mould or something like – and my boyfriend’s like, what on earth are you doing? And I’m like oh, oh, I wonder – and it’s just once you know about processes and things, you start picking stuff up in – I used to think my DT teacher was a complete nutcase but you do start to pick stuff up and look at it, and I don’t take things for granted anymore. But there’s lots of politics and legislation and things involved as well and it’s not just a case of go away and draw a pretty picture and make it – which I think a lot of people think it is. It’s all kind of like, well, this directive’s come in and you can only use x grams of polymer and things like that. It’s tricky, but if industrial design wasn’t around, a hell of a lot of people would notice it – ‘cos they wouldn’t have anything to sit on mainly! Things like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what characteristics do you think make a good designer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Ooh, do I have to have them?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: No more like an ideal.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: An ideal – communication skills definitely, from sourcing out needs and wants, to presenting the ideas and communicating with manufacturers and things, because even now, having to ring up manufacturers and things and say, how do you make this? How do you make that? And then the lads are saying well, they won’t tell me, but they’ll tell me and so I use it to my advantage then, but…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That was one of my next questions.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, so communication, confidence – definitely, to design something and within the DT department it’s a harsh world, to design something and stand by it all the way through, and even have the lecturers going hmm, ok that’s a bit different – so I’m not conformist, not at all that’s boring. And er, to be able to stand by it – even if it falls flat on its face – to still say, well, you know, it’s obviously the world’s not ready for it quite yet and just to pull yourself together. Erm, a love of sleep deprivation (laughter) and to put your work first – definitely – because my life is DT, and that’s really sad, but it is and everything else, apart from family, comes second. And even family – well, you know, if you’ve got a major project, then who knows? But erm…I don’t know – a good sense of humour. If things go wrong you need to be able to laugh about it, and to get on with people as well. And you have to be quite adaptable as to who you get on with even if people are annoying the hell out of you. You’ve still got to be OK with them, because you’re gonna see them everyday, just like in the workplace – you’ve got to er – if people get stressed out, as they do, and tetchy and things go wrong, and they start snapping at you – you’ve just got to take it on the chin and leave them be.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah – do you have to do a lot of group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. I hate it – I really hate group work because I always end up being a leader, which is my fifth one, being good at leadership – you sometimes have to take over – and I don’t like it because I always end up doing more work, but I can’t stand people dawdling. It really, really annoys me. And like ooh well, and I would say it’s mainly the girls – not all of them but there’s a certain section of girls, who hang together, who dither. And it’s not their personality, it’s just the way girls are I think. I mean they always ask the lads for opinions before they do things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Like they don’t have confidence in their own work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Exactly. And it’s – why not – why can’t they be so confident and you’re completely, you know, wiping the slate clean again – I have to build it up again, but they’re oh, what do you think? Oh I don’t know. Did you watch Neighbours? And it’s like they really let the side down – they really, really do. So you need to have the guts to – it’s all about guts really. You just need to stand up there and say right, this needs to be done. You’re gonna do it and you’re gonna do and it’s just like, deal with it, basically.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that there are advantages to doing group work though?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm, yes, yes because you learn, at school, there are advantages to group work but in practice no, I hate group work. I like group work, in the fact that it gives me – I feel personally responsible for my own work because I’m guaranteed to do – to the absolutely best capability that I can do. If it’s just me, you know, I’ll leave bits that I really shouldn’t do but it’s OK. I know the difference between – you know – like a 40% OK if I’m tired, like and 70% group work. So I tend to put more effort in because I don’t want to be the one that brings the group down, but at the same time it’s usually me saying right then, so I seem to be always the one that’s trying to enthuse everybody and I don’t like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think the fact that you have done so much group work, do you think that will help you when you go into the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it’s actually making me less tolerant of people. As I’m going along I seem to be stuck with problem people, because right the way through since starting I’ve always been classified as the ‘good girl’ that would put people on the straight and narrow and there’s always a naughty boy sitting with me at my table, at primary school, so I could have this wonderful, angelic effect on them. But erm, I don’t know, it’s – I think it’s the way that people handle pressure that’s the big crunch for when it comes to group work, in DT because I’ll be – I feel it, blooming heck I feel it, and I don’t have much sleep and sometimes I burst into tears for no reason, but not when there are lads around. And er, it’s just – for group work it’s just like I’m like the face on it, it’s kind of like you know, we can do this and positive talk and I talk myself out of it. But, if I’m put with people who are ‘oohh, how many pages did you do?’ And ‘what colour’s your folio?’ And yes, they do go that low – then I’m like who cares? You know. And it’s like ‘well I’ve done 60 pages’ and it’s like ‘oooh’. And yet they’ll have somebody really like kind of ‘what type font – space are you using? What size font are you using?’ And it’s stupid – it really is. That’s when the group work really irritates me – it’s people discussing little, tiny things instead of doing the work, and they always get distracted. And if there’s a lad he’s like, oh did you watch the rugby last night? Oh you going to [student union event]? And if it’s a girl it’s like, oh did you watch Neighbours? Oh what did you think? Ooh, what’s gonna happen? Oh I’m so stressed out, my boyfriend says this and it’s like, I just don’t talk about my boyfriend in DT at all. Like with a couple of close friends in DT, I did – admittedly, but if there’s group work to do, I do the group work because I don’t want to do in the evening – my free time is when I want to spend time with my boyfriend. I’ve just finished a bad group work project, so that’s not a good question right now.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, going back to the characteristics – do you think that any of the characteristics are more male or female characteristics?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, because, this is my mum’s upbringing now – this is dreadful – I sound like my mum, but – I’ll have to explain my family history - my mum and dad got divorced when I was 5, my mum suddenly became very feminist and she said you can do anything, don’t end up like your dad and so I’ve always had it drummed into me, confidence and things like that. But I don’t think that any characteristic has to be necessarily female or male.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that other people probably perceive that it is and that’s why there aren’t so many women in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s something that I think – sometimes I feel like a fly on the wall, because sometimes I think the lads forget I’m a girl. Like oh, phew, oh and things like that and it’s like OK, fair enough. And I think, to be honest, because I’ve been with my boyfriend now for a year and a half, if I was single – like completely single – then I think I’d be viewed slightly differently, but I think I’m – being just safe at the moment and allowed into that group because I’m not going to go oooh and start giggling in a corner, but – some of the lads – like last year were definitely surprised that girls were doing things and that girls were confident, because I don’t have problems with presentations and like – some people, male and female, like presentations, some despise them and start shaking and passing out and stuff and last year we did a big presentation and my partner was the tallest, big captain of the rugby team - really tough, popular guy and he was lovely – he was a real softie but he actually fainted, in the middle of the presentation, and I was just there talking away because I imagined my mum sat at the top, near the exit sign, and just concentrate on her, type of thing. But I think that’s just schooling as well just the way you’re taught things and I just heard umph, and he was there on the floor and he’s still getting ridiculed for it, but if it was a girl I don’t think she would be ridiculed. But because it wasn’t expected from him, but, there’s a lot of preconceptions, a lot of people are like, oh you do woodwork, oh – and they always look at my nails, which aren’t bad – still got spray paint on some of them but – ‘oooh, and your nails are quite long. Tell me do you wear pink? And there does seem to be this preconception if you do engineering or a science degree or whatever then you’re a butch lesbian basically and that really irritates me – because I’m not, you know. I’m bubbly and I’m happy and I’m just – not that butch lesbians can’t be bubbly and happy, but you know? I don’t think that sexuality has anything to do with capabilities.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, but there’s this perception that women and engineery type things don’t go together and if they do you can’t be feminine?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: But some of the things the lads in DT come out with and they forget that I’m there, they’re all like oooh, all girls who do engineering oh they’re all plain and they’re all boring. It’s like all girls who do DT oh they’re either super duper arty or just you know, keep themselves to themselves. And it’s like well, where do I fit in to all of this? You know – oh well, they kind of have that look on their face like to say Katie was here, damn.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that about the other girls though sometimes?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Definitely – definitely. I don’t know there’s – everyone’s got the right to dress, to act whether – do what you need as long as it doesn’t do harm to another what I believe in basically – but some of them, they’re just like mullet hair – mullet hair styles – girls with mullets, for God’s sake why? And they’re walking round looking like they’ve been attacked by a strimmer with you know like eye shadow – like eye shadow going and over the eyebrows and everything – that’s – they look like they’re in the middle of a Vivienne Westwood fashion show and stiletto heels, in the department when you’ve got to walk between – it’s just not practical, and I think what are you doing? But some of the lads to be honest, some of the lads are very, very preened and if they got their hands dirty – you know – well, it would kill them and they all wear perfect hair, but the lads is just as stereotypical as the girls. Definitely, because they all fit into either surfer, or arty or Mr Popular lad who’s always been in the sports team – a bit of a player and then there’s the quiet ones and I’ve got a problem with the sporty ones because they’re very, very arrogant and it’s their confidence – girls are – because I can put my work up on the wall and say oh yeah, and all my mates are like oh yeah its really good, and I’m thinking you’re only saying that because you’re my friend, thanks but – and you say it back to them – but think hmm. And then, a lad’ll come along and say that’s rubbish. You could do better than that and it’s – but at least it’s an honest opinion. And it’s – I don’t know – it’s – then you get lads coming in, and it is the lads to be fair – the big, tall lads especially, who are put up the work and they sit there and go yeah, look at that. And they’ve just – they’re loving themselves completely, and I can sit there and smile and think, yeah, that’s OK, inside I’m thinking I should have done this, I should have done that – Oh God, she’s done that too (Sharp intake of breath) you know, and it’s a face worse than death if they’ve got the same coloured mount board and other worries like that. But then some of them just sit there and go yeah – you know, they’re just smoothing out their T-shirts and things and that’s – oh, that annoys me. It’s one thing being confident but it’s another thing when, you know, they’re walking about – yeah. I think the best invention would be kind of like a headband with a mirror in front so they’re permanently surrounded by beauty – it’s just – and they are bitchy. And some of the lads are worse than the girls, about everybody in general and it tends to be the lads who slag off the teachers, rather than the girls. I think that’s kind of a male struggle and like sons and fathers – who takes the power and things like that. But there’s lots of very heated arguments and it’s all to do with – well, I think they’re pissing up trees – they’re marking out territory. In a department like that where you can have a little workspace – like lots and lots of – I don’t know whether you’ve been in there or not? (No) Lots and lots of big work benches and you go in and you junk your stuff, you do your work, go out, come back after lunch, you come in, you have to work round whatever with dreaded freshers or finalists – which are a bit scary – and you just have to get on with it. And then, in lectures anybody sits with anybody basically – ‘cos of all the group work we all know, like somebody’s worked somebody, so therefore they must be OK. But then the big groups come in and they have to sit together, even if there’s like 2 spaces and there’ll be 6 lads, and it’s all the preening lads, have to stay in that one tiny space standing in the model of this little circle because they just can’t be separated. Because, if they’re separated – they’re nice when they’re separated (yeah) but they’re really, really quiet and it’s oooh, it’s so daft. But I think I had the bad habit of speaking my mind and like one person like – oh why are you sitting over there? It’s like oh are you scared of boy germs and I’m just like well why are you all crouched together, you know, what’s going on? Just be yourself. Like today I was erm I went in and most of my friends – ‘cos Friday’s a horrible day when I have to do mechanics in a morning with 23 lads and 3 other girls, one of whom [name] – I think you’ve already interviewed her – is my friend, and she’s – so we often sit in there and it’s like can you do this one too? Yeah, can you? In the afternoon though, all the other girls and some of the lads are all doing artefacts or sustainable design, so I went on my break – I went in this afternoon, knowing full well that none of my friends, my close friends would be in there. And, it was packed out with blooming freshers spraying paint all over the show, not taking advice, you know, just doing what they want to do. I’ve just finished beautiful spray painting model and it’s wonderful and it’s perfect and it’s going to get ruined before the hand-in date and oh this, they just stood there freely talking away – you feel like crouching over it like its your little child, you know, to defend this wonderful work that you’ve worked so hard on, and I had to sit on a table with finalist – finalist lads. Finalist lads are lovely. I have to say they’re better looking than lads in my year, but they’re – personality wise – it’s like oh, hiya, oh what’s your project? And they’ve never talked to you before and you’re like – and you start asking them – oh if I were you I’d do it this way instead, which is so different from my year. I think it’s just my year, to be honest. But everyone’s competing with everybody. If you have them on your back, the wrong coat, if you talk to the wrong person, because so and so said this to so and so and I know there’s going to be a certain element of that, on every course, but I think because my course is such an expressive course as well – everyone wants to be heard, everyone shouts over everybody else and I just get to the stage where I’m shut up, you asked me a question – listen.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, you’ve maybe said a bit about this already but what are the main advantages and disadvantages to being a woman in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, for myself? (yeah) Advantages – erm because it is a male dominated industry, lots of the men are very, very tempted to help you, if need be. Some of them for more genuine reasons than others.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you find that quite patronising?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. It annoys me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you let them help you or not?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It depends. It depends how stuck I am. If I’m really, really stuck then – because now obviously in the 2nd year I know who’s (that way?), but if I’m really stuck and there’s no one else, then I put up with it because – especially if their marking your work, you know, you have to do basically, because you can’t go up to a well established lecturer and say I don’t like the way you’re speaking to me. Because they’re just gonna go right, you know, goodbye. And you’ll get marked down. And that does happen, a great deal. (Really?) Yeah, and er – other advantages – I think that there is a certain and with all the members of the staff, all the people in the industry, there’s a certain amount of respect as well, because they know that you’ve come through the ridicule and you’ve come through the, ‘alright love?’ and sometimes it’s like being in a builder – you know, when you walk past a builder’s yard, ‘ooh aye, love’ an stuff like that and you just think… I don’t know – the disadvantages is that I think that women are generally better at communication than men. And I think some of the men feel a bit phased if a woman goes up to them and says (?) so and so, you know, this plywood, this thickness – you know – ahhh, this has been here – ahhh, they just go uhhhh, no. too much information, you know, but…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think they feel threatened by the fact?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think some of them do it depends how strong the character are themselves. Disadvantages are that usually, erm in the department as in lads, like the year below, they tend to – because I’m not obviously pretty covered up or whatever, and I’m not the least attractive girl in a labcoat, then you do get like physical attention as well, which again, you get anywhere. They’re like ooooooooh yes, she’s a hot! You know if you’re welding or something, its like ooohhh and especially since the er – the Benny Benassi video came out, I don’t know if you’ve seen it or not (no) and there’s like all these wonderful women who’ve all had cosmetic surgery, dungarees and machinery and stuff – ever since that, ooooh, you know, why aren’t you like this? Why? Why would I want to be? You know, I have no intention of going to be seen in a bikini and dungarees. So then – in a way I think that the stereotyping and the – the wariness on behalf of men, is making me stronger because I go into situations – I don’t go into situations, don’t get me wrong, I don’t go into situations expecting trouble, or expecting to be patronised but I treat them as equals. If they’re patronising then the tables change slightly but I’m more confident in who I am because I have had that kind of bullying element that you – especially from the lads at school. You know, it was kind of like, oh, you’re a girl, what are you doing here? You know, you don’t belong here – type feeling and you feel a bit of an outsider, but I think that was because I was the only one in the class, but…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you deal with it when they’re making comments and stuff?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It depends, depends who they are. Erm, if it’s stuff like lovey and things – that doesn’t bother me so much, because, I was in [shop] a couple of weeks ago and a bloke on the till said thanks, duck, and because I’m from [area], I’m not used to being called duck – I mean why would you call someone duck? You know, and it’s like thanks, duck and I don’t see it as a term of endearment or like cheers love, you know, thanks love that type of thing. I sort of saw it as oooh, and because I was buying drill bits as well. Again that kind of – you know – has she got the right type sort of look – [shop] is the worst but I’ll get on to that in a second. And er, I like – why are you calling me duck? And so I was like stressed out – it was immediate offensive but it just really – if it’s lads that – I did sixth form, ‘cos we were in class of 4, which was wonderful and they’re like – but there were 3 other lads, one of whom is now here but doing engineering, he still really kills me – jokingly, he reassures me, but erm they’re like Oh God, you’re using a band saw and it’s like oh yes, and you just – you end up bantering back at them, like oh mind your forehead near the band saw, you know, you might cut off something and things like that and then you go whooooooo, until they tend to go, I’ve just got what you mean and it’s like ah ha. But, you learn to deal with things the lads way, and if you can stick up for yourself, the lads way, rather than showing that sometimes it hurts, and sometimes you think why are they picking me on me? You know – I’m only a girl. And sometimes you think, I’m a girl, leave me own, why are you picking on me? I’m not a bloke. But you – you still – if they’re mouthy with you, you’re mouthy back and according to schooling, it’s not ladylike, and it’s not proper but that’s the way you get through things and you don’t get through life being lovely and nice with people. And if people try and mess you about, sometimes, depending on who they are, you have to stand up for yourself. It’s like if someone on the street came up to you and started giving you a load of abuse it’d be girl, you wouldn’t put up with it, so why should you put up with it in the department? Especially you shouldn’t put up with it in the department, because the fact is I know I got higher ‘A’ levels than some of the lads, if anything I’ve got more right to be there, which is a really good thing to throw at them and it makes them feel really insecure and we start playing with their hair – and they’re looking down at the floor. But er – turn the boys into nervous wrecks but erm, you just have to throw it back at them. And [shop], I had to go in for spray paint for my project, and 3 blokes on the counter, ‘oh you buying this for your boyfriend’s car love?’ – I’m like, ‘no, it’s for a project at university.’ ‘You do art then?’ Like, ‘no’.
