I do design technology – like oh right, OK, yeah, good. So are you sure you got the right paint. Now are you using the right filler primer? Are you sure? Have you read the instructions? Now mind it near your clothes? And there was another lad from my course, a couple of tills down, very, very similar group of men, serving them because I had to be a youth, to be employed – and er, they’re going (?) and I’ve done this, ‘are you sure?’ ‘Well I’ll give you the receipt lovey, just in case you change your mind’. And I’m thinking, it’s a can of paint – you know – I think I can choose a can of paint. So there’s still definitely that element. And it’s always like – like my friends team, like ooh, did [boyfriend] go and do that? Did you get [boyfriend] to paint that? Ooh. I’m like why? He’s rubbish at stuff like that, why would I give it to him for God’s sake?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, has the course been what you expected it to be?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, it’s been a helluva – er, no, it really hasn’t been, in that the prospectus – I mean one thing it’s sunny in the prospectus which is not there.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I don’t think they take photos in the rain.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: They must have waited 364 days to take that photograph. But er – actually from ‘A’ level DT you realise the amount of work you have to do. And from A levels on the whole, you realise the amount of work you have to do and the commitment you have to have. Erm, when it comes to the prospectus describing Design Technology it’s like, oh you get so many hours of work per week and now comes the decision that that amount of time is based on a lecturer who’s been locked in a room, and who’s been teaching the subject for 20 odd years, because there is no way that you can do all the work that we’ve got to do – and they’ve managed to position our deadlines perfectly so we’ve got phys – like deadlines, during revision week and during exam week because we don’t have a revision week. Everyone else in the university does but we don’t. And you don’t expect that. It’s wonderful – you get so many set projects and you think it’s going to be set out nice and evenly but there are times, in DT, where you can’t really do anything and today I’ve literally sat waiting for paint to dry. And that’s really frustrating because you know you’ve got to do it, but still, you sit there thinking I could be doing this, but you can’t touch it ‘cos it’s still wet. And I made the forepart today for it, is it dry? But I don’t know – it’s – I think it’s just particularly my course, but there’s – obviously it’s competitive but because it is so competitive and because every time you submit a piece of work you can hear people going – oh did you see so and so? Oh, God, I wouldn’t have handed that in, would you? Everyone’s trying to steer you on the same way. And I was kind of going to the lads, well, actually I think it was alright, because if it was my work I’d be gutted if I heard someone talking about me like that. So hopefully – it’s a bit of a front, because I’d only do that so they won’t talk about me, because they’ll know I’ll come back and face them if I hear about it. But yet again that’s a bit of male bravado, in a way. Trying to give this big macho image of, so that nobody tries to tackle you, it’s all about protecting yourself from criticism, but the course is a lot more competitive than I expected it to be and it’s the nasty level, and there are really, really, really nasty people who do not want you to succeed and just decided they don’t like you, for whatever reason, whether you’re a girl, or whatever – just because. They must sit at home at night, thinking right you know, today I’m going to focus on this one person, but I love it to bits and I wouldn’t change it but I do have a love/hate relationship with the department and some days I’ll leave the department and not be bothered if I ever go back again, and others I want to get straight back in there and am really enthusiastic.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you been taught by any female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. Oh, only a few – very, very few. There was one in the department, who’s gone to Iowa, which I’m not happy about er called [name] who – she actually persuaded me to apply here – not directly but on the Open Day she was so full of life and she was like you’re a girl, get over it, come on. Really, really up for life basically – really lively, really, really lively and really talented, so she’s like oh, you’ll see from the reading list they’re all written by me, and things like that. It’s like go girl and the lads are like, ‘she’s written a book’ and its like no she’s actually written 12, and – but I was aware – because obviously there’s like office politics between the lecturers but you can see the male lecturers are treating her differently than each other and she was outside of them, but she just didn’t really bother but she put some of the teenage lads to absolute shame. She was like why on earth are you wearing that? Do you think you’re going pull? You’re not. And things like that, really down to earth. Most of the lads, interestingly enough, hated her. But I really respected her, if I ended up just like her, I’d be totally happy. But there’s another lady who teaches, in engineering, who’s the complete opposite of [name]. And she’s er – I don’t want to say plain because she’s not plain she’s very highly intelligent, she knows her subject – ‘cos I don’t like judging people by what they look like, but she’s highly intelligent – she knows her subject but she isn’t all pink and girly, you know. But, she knows her stuff and she’s not gonna put up with any rubbish in the lectures. If the lads, at the back, start playing up, she goes, ‘shut up’. You’re only, you know, empty vessels make the loudest noise – just like that, she’ll shut them up – no problem. And they’ll listen to her but they don’t respect her and I think it’s a problem with – I know height – height doesn’t matter, but it’s like but it tends to be the bigger lads. Not, the old lads, it’s just the bigger lads who have a problem with female lecturers. And everyone else seems to be OK. But some of our – we’ve got a lady who teaches ergonomics in our department, now, and she’s so quiet. And she looks like if you say anything to her she’ll cry. And, want to hand you’re work in on time, so you don’t upset her, kind of thing but the lads really don’t want to go anywhere near her because she has such a fragile – you know – little bird type image. Whereas with [name], you know, you wouldn’t dare hand your work in late because she would kick your ass – you know – she would come out, inside the foyer, which is a bit like the common room I suppose and be like, ‘why haven’t you handed your work in’ in front of everybody and she was, you know, she was cool. But there was – she had lots of problems with the lecturer that I now have problems with and I think the fact that I obviously respected her a great deal, because I started my course late, I was 3 weeks late, because of the ‘A’ level mis-marking. They marked my Physics with a U instead of a B (Oh my God) So I started off on the foundation engineering course – for my first 2 weeks and fought my way in. But the lecturer who I have problems with, mentioning no names, turned round to me and said no, we can’t –he’s the admissions tutor, so you can work that one out - said no, you can’t come in end of story and that’s it and then the Head of Department, later phoned up and I was distraught – I really, really was ‘cos I hated the Foundation Engineering course because of the male lecturers, and they were really, really sexist, they were like ‘now can the girls manage this?’ and it really was that bad. And I was like, yes, I can still manage to use a calculator but I nearly left university because I just couldn’t stand the course and then got changed over – but [female lecturer] had problems with the lecturer anyway, and I think because I obviously showed her such a great deal of respect – I try and avoid this lecturer as much as I can because I’m over my anger but I still have real issues with him because he had no right - he didn’t go through the proper rules and regulations at all. Because there hadn’t ever been such a big mix up – with grades - there weren’t really any rules to follow but he didn’t like consult the right people – he just told me straight off no, come back next year and you might get a place, and from being at a school where you had to go to a first division university – if you don’t go to a first division university, people stop talking to you. That’s how shallow some of them are and it’s like the horror that you may – you know – what are you gonna do – it’s like you psyche yourself up so much and you’ve decided who you’re gonna stay with in different weeks when you arrive at this university and the horror that you’ve got to wait another year for it after you’ve built yourself up for it, so I’m still reasonably miffed with him. But he still has the attitude that he favours the really arrogant lads and I think probably because, at university he was one of them. So he sees them as his chums and they are mates and that strikes me as being really strange because with the rest of us, with the quiet lads, and with the girls he is really, really fierce and one of those people you can’t ask for help, because if you ask for help he’ll ridicule you and he’ll say, in front of the entire lesson, oh so and so asked for help and it’s like (laughs) because they have to laugh to go along with him, so they’re not the next one to be ridiculed so he is a bit of a bully but – I’ve only got another year of him, so there you go.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s quite interesting. Would you find it encouraging then to have more female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, but only if they were cool.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Like [name]? (yeah, definitely) I don’t think I’ve heard anyone say a bad thing about her yet.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s erm, I don’t know – she really had guts and she did what she wanted to do. And the nicest people – the nicest of males in the department are the technician staff, and the workshop staff because all of them – because when I first started – ‘cos I was 3 weeks late onto that course, of course I had to make new friends and everyone else had already gone into friendship groups. But fortunately they started to get bored with each other – so I was the new attraction – you know, like ooh, ooh she’s new…let her in our group. And then…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did that help you being a girl, because if you were a lad then they probably – ‘cos there is so many they probably wouldn’t even notice?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so. But a lot of the teachers on the course, it’d be good to say, oh we have a new girl – Katie here – where are you? Stand up and it’s like – so I’m just stood there going – Hi! I was introduced 400 times this week but I’m still here, you know. It’s really – it’s cringe worthy, but you’ve got to take it on. But if the female lecturers are confident enough – like we did have one, and she’s bolshy – she’s not confident, she’s just bolshy and she throws her weight around and cos she wears a skirt, she has the power, and that is definitely – that is the mentality she projects to people. Because she is female, therefore men should – I don’t expect men to hold doors, things like that. I’m quite happy to hold doors for lads on my course if they’re loaded up and they’re like oh cheers Katie, you know, whatever, but she’ll stand by a door and she’ll be like (sniffs) and things like that – it’s just pathetic, you know. If they’re like [name], then great, if not then they can stay out.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the male and female lecturers have a different style of teaching, or do you think it just depends on the individuals?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm (??) this is where I start going ooooh, engineering ooh. Design technology, yes, because female lecturers definitely explain things better and the male lecturers are like oh well this is this. Another – I don’t think – it’s probably just our department – doing our power point slides, they don’t elaborate, you know, da,da,da, da, da, da. And it’s like (?) you know and they don’t have intonations in their voice – most of them are (makes monotonous noise) whereas the females are more expressive and they’re in there and it’s like, oh last week when I was in Ikea and like, because they use practical examples, you remember it more easily. Whereas the males are like, mmm, you know, when I was in my garage, washing my car… and it’s just not fun. Whereas the engineering lecturers – they’re all the same. I’m sorry, but they are.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you got a personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are they male?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Male.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you happy with that – your personal tutor – would you rather have a female?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: He’s wicked – he really is. Erm, [name], he really is – I don’t know if I just talk to him because it’s kind of like the late start thing and – I have got over this by the way - but you know, it’s – he’s always said right, this is what happens, you know. This is where you go – and I got like the personal tour basically, but he looks out for – I really feel that he looks out for me. And I see him more as a final student, or a kind of big brother figure but he is fairly young – he’s only mid 20’s. But I see him more as a big brother kind of – someone to look after me and if I get really upset or really angry about something, I’ll just go and knock on his door and burst into tears and he’s fine with it. And he sits you down, passes you the Kleenex and says stop crying, please. Stop crying – I don’t know what to do anymore. Whereas, some of my friends’ personal tutors, I wouldn’t go anywhere near them because really in DT they see it, if you ask for help, it’s a weakness. And you’re failing and that’s not good and if you’re known to go to your personal tutor, then people are like oooh, what’s going on?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Does that all go back to being like a masculine thing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm, ‘cos it’s the girls who go to their personal tutors more than the lads. The lads are like OK, whatever, and carry on but there’s another guy – [lecturer] – who really persuaded me to do the BSc, ‘cos he’s a mechanics tutor and also head of my year at the moment and everybody else, when I first came, to the course – its stupid ‘cos I live in the same place and everything – but when I first arrived properly, yet again he really explained things to me, sort of a bit like a dad, in a very strange way, but he’s friendly and he understands things and he sits down and listens to you, whereas some of the lecturers, if there’s any hint that emotion is going to come into anything, then they do start backing away. But a lot of the lecturers, if you go into their rooms or whatever, they’ll either kind of leave of the door open or – yes, they have to watch their own backs but I don’t know – it kind of makes me…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that worries them?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah…I think…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Think women – coming into our…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Their male domain.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And now they’re gonna start doing us for sexual harassment.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well some of them should do – definitely but there was this one – I said all technicians are fine – but there’s one who helps the girls and not the lads. And you have to pay a small price for the help – of basically sitting there and smiling, and trying to look pretty but he was – like with electronics, last year, whereas all the girls had their hands up and all the lads had their hands up and he sits down and helps each of the girls, and asks how our work’s going and how we’re finding student accommodation and things like and ignores the lads completely and – but I think it gives them a bit of a wake up call, because we have that, lots of times – especially in engineering, where some of the lab technicians will help the lads and if I had a question, it’s like well, yeah, hmm and they does just to seem to like, kind of like, well, why are you asking this – isn’t it obvious to you? And I don’t know if that’s just me, walking round with a chip on my shoulder. I don’t think it is. I hope it isn’t – but they just demonstrate this kind of oooooh, it’s especially in engineering, oh it’s the DT girl, Oh God.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, who then do you think has been the biggest influence on you since you started the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Within the university?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah – well, no, not necessarily.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: My mum – well, joint place [female lecturer] – well, with mum doing it – erm, she sent a (??) to get me high marks. My mum, because my mum’s never stopped – let anything stop her do things and within the family, when my mum and dad got divorced, my grandma saw it as a disgrace – because my grandma’s very, very Jewish, and it’s a disgrace and divorce is not spoken about and isn’t it a problem that her daughter had a daughter and you weren’t supposed to speak about this big problem that had happened. So – my mum’s very, very independent – she probably thought that it – going to university, and she is – she does what she wants to do – she’s – not in a selfish way, but if she sets her mind on something, she does it. So, I have a lot of responsibility to myself to do well and to get through the course and to try and get a blooming first but at the same time, my mum sacrificed a lot to pay for my schooling and worked way too much to do that and put her own life on hold – because she wanted to go to university for years – but put her own life on hold so that I could have a good education. So, in a way, I feel I’m doing this – not to make her proud of me, but to – to show that her efforts have allowed me to achieve, basically. And if my mum can do university, then I can do university, even though she’s doing a BA, which we tease each other about, and we’re gonna graduate at the same time. It’s like she’s doing a 3 year course and it’s weird, but [female lecturer] because I arrived and the lads were like ooh, not only was there a girl doing DT, but it was the new girl doing DT. So there was like, what can she do? You know, trying to work out where I am on the pecking order and if I’m a threat, and if I’m single and all sorts of things like that, and can she use a band saw? And it’s like it’s a real big status thing– can you use a bandsaw? It’s pathetic – I’ve been using it since I was like, that big. But erm…but then I – I went to talk to - because it just seemed strange, after salvaging myself from the sixth form, the lads finally left me alone and just let me get on with my work – and suddenly as an equal, but – you know, it took me 2 years to do. And then, starting again was a bit de-motivating and suddenly having like a hundred and – I’m trying to work out how many girls there are on my course - about of 120 as a whole, I’d say about 90 lads – trying to persuade 90 that you can actually do stuff, or feeling that you have to and then [female lecturer] saying, well, you know, you’re doing this for yourself so I don’t see why you should have to prove yourself to anybody. You know prove yourself to yourself and I was like well, OK. And then I always came out with (?) with them, in those days, went home and thought ooh, it’s not that easy but – yeah, she has influenced.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, moving onto the placement then – do you think that you’ll use skills that you’ve learnt, that you will use on your placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Communication. Something like general studies and then I had this obsessive English teacher, saying communication is key and I had to repeat it so many times. It is – yeah it is basically communication because the placements vary so much. I went to an open day at [company] and based in [area], which is wonderful – I love the midlands – which isn’t a true northern thing to say, but erm – my mum would kill me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: People from the midlands think that it is north.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: True you know, it’s like people saying I’m from up North, whereas they’re from [town] – I’m like you’re not – rubbish. But, what was I talking about? Yeah, [company] and that placement’s managerial and I was looking round the actual plant itself, which is massive – they have a bus going round this blooming place which amazed me, I’d love to be in that environment with so many different people. But we went in the canteen and like everybody from literally the Chief Exec was sat there to the fork lift truck driver – they all mixed completely together. Lots and lots of women there, interestingly enough, but everybody seemed to be equal. And even though the managerial design job – mm, sounds a bit boring to me, there again its leadership, but the fact – the equality, or the sense of equality I should say, really appeals. And not having to try and establish yourself, in your own right, because you’re a woman, but other placements I’ve had interviews for, such as consultancies – smaller consultancies in London, where the only female in the office is the receptionist and they really don’t know how to treat you. It’s that kind of like, oh does she make the coffee or does she draw, and they’re like, maybe she doesn’t do both. Multi-tasking, women are meant to be good at this – but I often get the feeling that if I was a man, I would be treated so much differently in those situations. But part of me wants to have a placement, in a smaller consultancy just to try and convert a few people into the way of thinking that women can do just as well as men. So, I think each spaces are trying to express yourself, so you’re confident but not arrogant and I think that’s really hard because everyone’s got different perceptions of it anyway, but to try and make a few people respect me, in my own right, cos I don’t want people just to respect me because I’m a woman who does DT because I could be completely shocking at it. But I want them to look at my work and judge me as my – in a way, a sexless person so you know, whether it’s male or female who’s done the work just say yes, that is good or bad. So that’s what I’m hoping for from a placement.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you feel like you’re ready and prepared to go on placement now?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why not?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm ‘cos I need a suit. But erm, I don’t know – in a way, mentally, I feel ready but emotionally I don’t think I am. Because mentally I’m feeling old enough and I want the responsibility, I want to get out of the {D&T building] and live life and be able to watch evening television, which I haven’t done for 2 years, which is so sad – and to obviously have that bit of money as well, but just to have the set, kind of 9 to 5 or whatever, and leave something at the office, is going to be a luxury I would love for a year. But then, emotionally – I think to be honest I’ll get bored, because within the department, obviously you can choose who you talk to lots and lots of different people all the time, but I think within an – the placement environment, I’ll be set in a smaller team of people, probably end up, you know, like bonding within that small team, and I think I’d end up – it’d just be my luck to get stuck with people I didn’t like, but I think – it’s not really – I don’t like the kind of conversations you have where it’s kind of like oh you know, yeah, OK, and you don’t really have anything – you don’t have anything of interest to say, ‘cos you said it 2 weeks ago. But with different people, like they’ll love the big environment and you can talk to a lot of different people and it’ll be random things and if you’re in a bad mood you can talk to somebody as lively as you, if you’re in a good mood, you talk to somebody who’s lively again, to keep you in your good mood, but I’m not ready for the kind of – the close office politics of it all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that what appeals to you more about a bigger company?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I take it you don’t know where you’re going yet?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, what other sorts of things have you been looking for in the companies that you’ve applied to? Have you looked at like long-term career prospects or …?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, yes. Long term career prospects, company car – erm, definitely career prospects, definitely [company] because [company] is the first – I got all my CV’s ready in January, sent them all out, got hardly any response but I tackled one of the consultancies – male arrogance, we don’t need to ring you back, type attitude and that really annoyed me – but that I think that was just a generally courtesy as a whole, but erm within [company] the – obviously [company], at the moment, are going through some problems and they’re having to cut back prices and they’re cutting older members of staff, which I don’t agree with and which my mum’s very, very annoyed about, even though she’s nothing to do with [company], but such as she’s older, and she’s a mature student so now she has age issues and she keeps talking about those ‘young people’ at university – I’m like mum, I’m one of them. But I definitely enquired about that, but also things like erm sports teams, things like that. I’m not – like, you won’t see me running round the track every day but I’m not particularly sporty but it’s just the chance – I suppose with music at school, to meet people you work with.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, like a social thing.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, you usually meet with – so that, I mean like walking into a canteen, not knowing anybody, doesn’t daunt me. I don’t like it, but it doesn’t make me go (sharp intake of breath) I’ll eat my sandwiches outside. But I don’t know, I just like to know lots and lots of different people so it’s a good variety. But I’m looking – I’m looking for a job after university because there are so few or because they are so very specific, if I found a job I love, on placement, I’m gonna work my absolute the hardest to try and get that job afterwards. But erm, hmmm, the location as well does come into it, because I want to go back towards home home, because my Mum’s going to Connecticut, in September, ‘cos she’s doing an exchange programme – this is so (unfair?) – so the house is going to be empty and you know, from a practical point of view – accommodation costs are terrific – but, I don’t want to be back at home, where all my friends have gone to university – because I’m just not ready for that life – I don’t want to lead that life. But then, and then I’ve got friends who’ve got placements round here and my boyfriend’s got a placement in [town], but I don’t want to work in [town] so I’m trying to look for good travel prospects as well, in all of this, along with everything else and flexi-time and sick leave and paid holidays but also, ‘cos within [company] you have a mentorship scheme, which is obviously you can’t just let someone into your company and leave them but, you shadow somebody for the first couple of weeks and then you have to report to them and then you’re given your own projects, which is like DT, because if I had somebody watching over me, day in, day out, it would probably really irritate me because I’m just not used to it. Because this is your project, you do what you want, get on with it as long as you hand it in by this time. And if I had somebody watching every step, like why are you doing that? Then, I don’t know. But erm, I’m looking forward to placement but it’s the insecurity of not knowing where I’m going, at the minute, that’s a strain slightly. But it’s the girls who are more organised than the boys because they’re only just thinking about sending CV’s now – because DT is all late starters, so to speak with placement, they’re only just coming through now.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, I don’t think anyone’s got a placement yet, have they?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think about 3 in [company] and that’s it. But er now interview’s are starting to come through, and yet again people are more competitive. Like, why is she in a suit? Where is she going? Where’s (?) and oooooooooh, but erm the lads, are only just considering now what to put on their CV, but the lads are coming to the girls and saying how do you put this in, in English? And which pictures would you choose, ‘cos they’re aware that it could be a female looking at their CV’s as well. So they’re trying to – they’re obviously aware that there’s a different way of looking at things but they’re never gonna put it in straight English, they’re always trying to weave it round a bit.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Has the university helped much, in finding a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Should they have helped more?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, erm placement tutor is about as much use as a chocolate teapot at the moment, in that – in one respect I’m lucky, because he teaches me mechanics basically. He definitely looks after his own – his own mechanics students, so in that case, I’m in favour. And he slags off the BA students and things – he really does but he tells us in that embarrassing, humiliating type way where you just cringe, but with regards to [company], I said I wanted to go to the open day, which was a free for all, basically, and he said, no, no, no. I’m like why? He was like you can do better than this – And I’m like well I want a placement – I’m aware that they’re going and I want a placement and he takes a couple of weeks to send out placement emails, so you’ve got about 3 days left to apply and things like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Who is your placement tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: [Name] - and he’s awful. But he said to me, no, you shouldn’t apply to [company]. If you send me a CV, I’m not sending it. And me, being me, find out who’s taking the CV’s, caught the train to [place], and handed it to the guy and I was off, which, on the open day it was him who was showing us around; he’s a recruitment officer; so – and he knew my name, and he kept talking to me, asking me questions. So, in a way, I think I may have scored myself a job.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: But why should you have had to do that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: But why’s he doing that to me then? He does play God, with placements, and he decides what’s good enough for us, what isn’t good enough for us, who will enjoy which placement the most, who would enjoy which town the most and from sitting there, number crunching, there’s no emotion, there’s no expression whatever, in doing sums, so he doesn’t ever talk to us as normal people it’s all just like lecturer, student, mechanic. And he really hasn’t – I feel under a tremendous amount of pressure to find a placement myself, because I daren’t – I irritate him, I know I do, because I check that he has read my emails, I check that he has sent off my CV to so and so, ‘cos you have to send CV’s through him. I don’t see why but apparently we do so he can keep a record of it, somewhere, but he’s like why are you double-checking? But I don’t want to – this wonderful placement which I have this wonderful image of, which doesn’t exist probably, to slip away from me because he has decided –he’s taking parental roles in a way, and it really, really doesn’t go down well with me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What would you have liked to see the university doing then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Have [female lecturer] as a placement tutor. I think – the university as a whole – the careers centre – wonderful service. They don’t have a clue what DT is, but it’s a wonderful service, and it is a really – I’ve been in there with my CV and I showed [female lecturer] my CV and they said completely different things – so my CV’s somewhere down the middle, but they really – they know their stuff, obviously, and they get people placements but, as far as DT goes, because there is such a wide span – I’m going to generalise now - but if you do – automotive engineering for instance, you know you can work for manufacturers or whatever, and it’s to do with cars – with design there’s so much stuff you can do, and they pass all the responsibility on to [placement coordinator] and then he decides and I think basically – it’s not so much – I can see that the university’s trying to create security in a way and create people within the department that you’re supposed to be able to bond with to – and he is alright, he’s just got a very strange sense of humour and laughs at his own jokes all the while so it’s like, you can stop laughing now, but er I think it’s just his personality. I think he’s carrying out his job role with you – it sounds very patronising – to the best of his ability but communication – his communication skills are awful.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, whereas that is actually quite an important thing in that role.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm, and he’s – he comes across as being very abrupt and very like, you are not going to do this. Whereas, I think a female would say, well, if you want to you can do, but I think you’d be better suited doing such and such a thing. But he just presents it as dead end, you know, you’ve put all this effort in, now I’m gonna cut you short, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, In terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in 5 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I know where I see myself like in 40 years time. Erm, I’ve got a little of career plan going on in my head. 5 years time…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Go on then, tell me what your little career plan is?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, in 5 years time I’ll have finished university, I’ll be 2 years into employment – hopefully. I’d like to work for a large company or a large consultancy such as [company]. Because [company] are Italian, all male, and I’m English and I’m female and this seems like a really good place to try and crack. It just seems like a challenge and I go for a challenge rather than an easy route. So, working for a consultancy, building up my CV, paying off my student loan – that’s where I’ll be in 5 years time.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about in 10 years?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: 10 years time – nice house, Laura Ashley furniture – no that’s something I don’t want. Erm, settled down, probably marriage wise – because that is quite important to me, but my career will probably come first. But I’m aware that I don’t want to put my career first so much that one day I wake up and I’m 55 and I have no close friends or no relationship or anything.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that women do, or women are sort of expected to either choose between one and the other?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Definitely. For instance, my boyfriend’s mum, erm got a first in physics, at university, had a couple of years working with an offshoot of NASA – she’s wonderful. Now she’s a housewife and to me, she looks – ‘cos [boyfriend]’s got 2 younger sisters and of course, she’s got a husband as well – massive family – but now she’s a housewife and that’s – she makes wonderful apple pie and it’s really homely and it’s like walking into the Walton’s, it really is. And there’s that wonderful family atmosphere and you’re always welcome but she’s wasting all that knowledge – all that intelligence and hard work has gone to waste, whereas my mum like housework is boring, so she’d rather do her university work. And er, she’s the complete opposite, she’s like well why should I stay at home? You know – I’m female why should I stay at home though?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you can combine having family and having a career?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I’m gonna try to.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it will be more difficult for you, because you are in a male or masculine environment?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm, definitely, because with my boyfriend who’s like a year and a half, so according to him – this is now serious – and he’s talking about marriage, which is scaring me quite a lot. But he keeps saying oh, I’ll have to be a house husband. And I’m like yeah – why is this even not an option beforehand, but it’s – I’m dreading – this sounds awful – and I shouldn’t even have considered this yet, but I’m dreading being pregnant, in a work environment, because I’ll feel, I think, that I’ve already – if I have – overcome any stereotyping that exists, and then you’ve got this great big bump, in front of you, and then everyone’s gonna be naturally like softly, softly anyway, in case you suddenly go into labour on them but then, from the way I perceive like my mum’s friends and things who I’ve seen being pregnant and the way men react around them – they go (sharp intake of breath) she’s very emotional, type thing. I think that would be a complete nightmare and I’d rather take, you know, a year and a half, two years off work, rather than be in a work environment – a male environment whilst being pregnant.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, do you think taking time out though would have an impact as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, definitely but I can work from home.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You’ve just made me think actually saying how you’re treated when you’re pregnant, because in my previous job, a girl I worked with was pregnant and people in our organisation started to talking to her, I think especial – well, men probably more than women, that she’d never spoken to before, started oh when my wife was pregnant, she did this and we did that and it was like, you didn’t speak to me before, why are you suddenly being my friend?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Because they felt – like when I joined the course because I was the newby – people would be my friend ‘cos I was the newby – they didn’t know me, but of course, once they decided they decided I was a confident, opinionated person, a Gemini – Oh God. Then they were like click (snaps fingers) and some of them haven’t spoken to me, ever since, and I’m not hostile to that at all because fair enough, we’re just not compatible as friends. But, I can’t be doing with people pretending to be your friend because it should be – I want people to be honest with me and I’ll be honest with them, basically, otherwise there’s no point. But with regards to career plan, erm children do feature in it, but it’s that kind of moveable area. No more than 2 children I’ve decided, definitely, for body reasons, and for career reasons as well, because I do intend wear a swimsuit again at some point in my life. But as I said my pay off my loan and financial independence is very, very important to me and I don’t want to be married or live in sin, as my grandma would say, or anything before I can stand on my own 2 feet. I never want to feel financially dependent on a man. That is because of my mum and dad and I know it is but I don’t see any harm in that. But then, working – a company you know, get all the pension and stuff like that, and then get married, maybe have children – see what happens, you know, I may not be able to, there’s all these different things that you just never, ever consider – that’s ‘cos I was watching Hollyoaks it’s like oooooooohh she can’t have a baby. And you think, oh I don’t want to find out right now, it’s a bit inconvenient, I’ve got the (?) on, but then I’d go back to work, hopefully for the same company because I think companies are becoming more aware of maternity and now there’s paternity leave. You think oh, blooming heck, you know, but I think that would annoy me, having –dithering me around. It’s like go out, leave me alone but er – brutally independent - but then earn enough to allow the opportunity for my children to have the same education as myself, if need be, where my boyfriend and I disagree. ‘Cos he didn’t go to Grammar School and he’s quite anti – grammar school, sometimes, because they’re all snobs and because they’re all arrogant. I’m like well, hello? You know and he seems to have no clue as to the (?) and that all Grammar school girls are like that and they’re all in bubble gum pink, and you know, with their nails, and driving in their jeeps and stuff. And it’s like the number 7 bus is not a jeep, so there we go – it’s not gonna happen. But, I’d like to be able to provide – providing for my family is a very big issue with me, and I think that’s just cos of who I am and the way I’ve been brought up and at school as well, it was a case of women should always be the bread winner. We should bring in the food, because why should men? And the thought of me ever having to ask my husband for money (yeah) [boyfriend]’s parents do that and she asked to – she’s given a weekly allowance for food and bills and then her own pocket money. If I’m working I’m not going to be given ‘pocket money’. You know, if I’m earning 30 grand and I’m going to say – be hopeful - per year, I’m not going to be passed off with 50 quid a week. No way. But if my children don’t want to go to university that’s up to them. I’ll encourage them to because I’m aware of the benefits – I’ve had them drilled into me since I was like 3 years old, but a lot of my family are in the services and things like that so I’m aware that they’ve all got well established, respectable careers and then, after they’ve settled and they’ve flown the nest – it’s gonna be 2 girls and they’ll marry lovely rugby players, who’ll play for England, and be friends with Johnny Wilkinson.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: But they won’t be over confident?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Exactly. And then I might set up my own consultancy, in London, and employ female designers – only – which is a bit – I don’t know if companies will actually…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Oooh that’s sexist?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It is sexist but you need to be – I think you need to be very, very sexist in the other direction, to even mildly balance out – everything else out, and have a – I would love to have a male receptionist. I know that’s very Sex and the City, but I don’t see why it has to be kind of like the teenage girl, just out of college. You know, anybody can pick up a phone and hopefully type letters and stuff like that but I do want to, you know, come back as one of the [university] Alumni and er speak to [name] and whatever his name is – [Chancellor] that’s his name. And er, I was talking to (?) and he was like oh yes, and all the old boys gathered together. No, I want to – this is where I get very, very arrogant, I want a department named after me, plus I want to contribute back, in the same way as school, but I don’t want to be just like, oh, she was a graduate here, she got married – yeah, you know. I want to be yeah, she did this and she’s done that, and she’s done that and now she’s doing whatever. So I’m not going to go out quietly.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Going back to what your boyfriend was saying, like around Grammar Schools – don’t you think it’s funny how, even when people know someone that’s been in a situation or – they still hold those stereotypes, it doesn’t break them down at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: With [boyfriend] though, it’s a situation that his mum is a Grammar School girl and that’s why – she said to me, because you’re a Grammar School girl, that’s why you’ll be a good daughter in law – this was on the first meeting. And it was like – because [boyfriend] and I live away – he lives in [area], I live in [area], so it’s 3 ½ hrs away from each other, so I don’t see his parents that often, really, but that was after 6 months and I’m thinking oh – daughter in law? Erm, OK, with a smile, but his dad – his views come from his dad, definitely. His dad quite annoys me in some ways because his dad’s like, oh [name] yes, you only think that because you went to Grammar School. And he still goes on about it and then, I must admit, at 6 months I had a major sit down and think is this gonna happen? Is our relationship gonna be a repeat of this because I’m gonna end up bumping him off, basically. But every now and again it’s in argument he throws at me, like you’re too confident, you’re too cocky, you not all that, but I don’t think I am you know. Because I know the me that sits there with my work and thinks this is rubbish. And I really don’t want to put it up on the wall, tomorrow and I don’t want to hand this in because I’m gonna do so badly. And I’ve never failed anything, so you know, I shouldn’t feel like that even – if like I look at my work, I should in actual fact, be really arrogant and cocky but I’m not, because I have a lot of self doubt.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That totally sounds like my sister.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: But then, my mum’s like, don’t be stupid. What you on about? You got 69% - well, it’s not a first. Even if you get 70%, it’s not 80% and it’s not 100%. Of course, I’ve never, ever got 100% in anything, but – you know, I want to pass everything, but then if I just pass that isn’t enough for me, but to have someone – he’s OK – he’s quietened down about it, since my little outburst, where I did turn into cocky grammer school girl, with him, I really put him down in his place. I said he was lucky to be with me. So he’s – because he does chemistry, BSc, so he’s very – but he’s not a geek. And, he’s very – very, very intelligent, knows his work, but he does his work and leaves it. DT, you can’t do that – there’s always something else – literally always something else you can do. And he’s like oh, it’s your Grammar School training, it’s all the pressure, it’s competing, and it’s like well everything’s competitive in life, you just haven’t realised it yet. And I do come out with some stuff from school and it is a bit hmmm – I do come out with Grammar School things, I know I do. But, I try to stop that – it’s the opposite extremes because I came here with 4 lads, from [name school] and one of them’s going out with a girl from the local high school. And she is well known, for all the wrong reasons and I’m like what? You’re going out with her and gosh – and I sort of said without thinking, hang on she’s not [name school]. And then like if I heard someone say that I’d think Oh my God, shut up, but obviously somewhere, deep within, that’s what I think but it’s exactly how the lads reacted when I started going out with [boyfriend] – it’s like he’s not [name school], he’s not even Grammar School, so of course he’s got a [area] accent as well – he doesn’t speak properly and it’s like – but he’s genuine, and that to me over rules and his [area] accent’s quite cute but that overrules everything else, to me anyway. But I value things such as (??) that I value things like Lotuses, and Porsches and Ferraris and things and I go past the Ferrari garage on the way to the train station and nearly miss my train and things like that. And he’s like oh you’re impressed by the money, you’re impressed by material wealth – most people probably think that. Most people probably look at cars and think oh, ooh yes, look at those alloys, or sorts of things like that but then I see it in the way that someone’s achieved something for themselves and managed to earn that for themselves, rather than that must have cost them 147 grand.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Not they must have won the lottery and give up work.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, especially if there’s a female driving it, and it’s like yeah, come on. And (??) in [town], one of those great big main roads, just as you go into the shopping centre, by the train station and there was lots and lots of sports cars and Audi TT’s stuff going about and if there is a female driver, the men they go (silent) because it is unusual. And it shouldn’t be. And they come out with it’s probably her husband’s car and – but I’m not gonna get annoyed with him about that, because that’s the view he had drummed into him, just like my views where it’s probably her car or the wife letting him drive it. So, hmm, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, almost at the end. What 5 words would you use to describe the design and technology industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The industry itself or the department?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How different do you think that the department and the …?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it will be worse in industry. Really. 5 words to describe it – competitive, erm demanding, mentally and physically rushing around, carting round heavy materials – you turn into Xena (tv character).. Erm, what else is there? Erm, I think it’s a hard question – concentration – because, it’s very easy, when you’re drawing something and when you’re designing something that you have to stick to what the person wants rather than what you think that they want and it’s very easy to get carried away and just end up designing something, looking at the end and thinking that’s got absolutely nothing to do with them. And a lot of our projects and a lot of real life design briefs are like for blind people and things like that, and you suddenly realise the colour of it doesn’t really make that much difference if they totally blind, whereas it’s more to do with texture and you’re actually forced to deal with things that you don’t usually look at it and it’s like this colour, you like that colour, you buy that product rather than something else you know. Er, 2 others – you need to be determined in yourself. You need to have really strong self belief she says, after making herself sound so insecure, or at least the impression of self belief. I think that’s different from confidence – confidence is something you project, self belief is something you feel. And to know that whatever happens you’re gonna be OK. And then I am usually like that – those placements and not knowing where I’m going, that’s thrown me completely, because I just literally don’t know what I’ll be doing in a couple of months time and I could be here, I could be abroad, and that’s definitely putting a strain on several different areas of my life. And the final thing – does it have to be 5?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I think I’ve …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you use masculine as well as then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. I probably would. You have to – it’s hard to like – you have to stereotype females to stereotype masculinity, in a way, but in an ideal world I would like to think of myself as being calm, collected, reasonable, diplomatic, can’t – like speak when you’re spoken to type person, you know but general chatty (yeah) and friendly person. Erm, masculine world with detailed deadlines, vicious person who snaps at people, who’s very moody – very, very moody – I shouldn’t be so moody, and I expect the same amount of hassle from other people as they expect from myself. And if they don’t give me 100% in anything, you know, it’s like – if people are late – and it’s not so much – that’s ‘cos I’m always early as you’ve experienced - but no it’s been people are really late yeah, isn’t it (?) – it’s all about respect basically and if I know that I’ve slogged at a piece of work and I’ve stayed up late – and you can tell because I look like death – and they come in and they’re talking about [student union events] ohh it was so wonderful and that’s not to say they haven’t done the work, she says (lost words) but I always get the sense that I do more work than other people. Perhaps not – just different work ethics in that I probably push myself too hard and one day I’ll probably burn out, so there you go.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the situation will improve for women in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not unless – I sound like my Mum again, it’s quite scary – erm not unless there are more females in power within Government I would say, because well it’s like the political situation – not that I’m into politics, but like President Bush, he has to get a speech writer to write all his speeches. If anyone asks him a question that he hasn’t prepared for, he can’t communicate an answer. Tony Blair, obviously highly influential man barrister you know, and knows the ins and outs and everything but they say – it’s like Margaret Thatcher – even though people love her or hate her, yes, she seems to be very forceful and there are lads on my course that are, oh you’re a Margaret Thatcher, aren’t you? You’re very forceful. I’m afraid not – but I don’t know. I think that if there were more not outspoken, I’m not talking about Germaine Greer type people, but people like Anita Rodderick – Body Shop lady – are people who’ve really achieved something for themselves – if they were publicised as much as men who have achieved – like Richard Branson – I’m sick of hearing about him, yes, he got in a hot air balloon and he didn’t fly, you know, but he still somehow fell into success. I honestly believe if it was a woman, it would be ridiculed, and she’d never be heard of again. And things like with – it comes even as low as David Beckham, with Victoria and how the press are gunning in on all the controversy and everything, but no-one’s actually seen the fact that this woman here is – it’s awful, even for it to be suggested – I haven’t seen even one report that’s even slightly seen it from her point of view.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: No, everything’s just slagging her off. How does she still be parading in public?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, and how she left him and that’s probably with my family background, and my mum and dad, and the fact that my dad is an older, fatter, David Beckham. In fact much older and fatter, and with a lot less hair but I don’t think that women are given equal rights within publicity and in politics, even though they’re supposed to be. The women that seem to be high profiled in politics are – and I can’t remember her blooming name now – Anne Widdacombe, big battle axes and they’re not – you don’t see any young or pre – I’m not saying that women are hardly ever pretty, but you don’t see any young, pretty women getting out there and really doing anything or they are but it’s just not being talked about. Because – especially, Government in a way is a bit like DT there’s a lot of old establishment – the old boys who went to the old polytechnics and things and they all went to – you know – they were all together and they remember the good old days, and there’s a woman ooooh and I think people are to eager to please them – to conform, because nothing ever changes if you conform all the time. I’m not saying have a complete female outburst but things in industry will only change if women get high profiled in the media and politics, because within media, like the most – I’m trying to think of who I can think of in the media in the last couple of years is things like Louise Woodward, things like that. Women don’t seem to be publicised for – it’s like the fact that she was female and she was a nanny – very female role – and so that she didn’t fulfil accordingly, to the story – didn’t fulfil her female, nanny, maternal role or like erm sexual harassment cases all over the place. And that only – that seems to get more coverage than like you know, this is the girl that came up from nothing and now she’s doing this and it’s all about how women seem to be tripping up. If Beckham scores a goal, it’s all over the front pages. You know good old Johnny Wilkinson – I mean I understand, but still it’s all over the entire place. But it’s like women’s football, women’s rugby, stuff like that, you just don’t hear about that at all, and I think that’s probably because there were men high up within the media as well, like the media hierarchy, rather than the women. So I think it’s just – it’s a gradual process I think it’s going to take many, many, many, many years for it all to slowly start filtering through. But I don’t know – there’s lots of views on it, it’s just it annoys me because you can only get so far before you hit another barrier of people – another row of opinions, and at the minute I’m getting a bit fed up with having to justify myself to people because I am who I am and men are allowed to be tired and stressed out – it doesn’t mean it’s the time of the month, it doesn’t mean that they’re having a bad hair day. Girls in DT have to tie their hair back – bad hair days everyday - and stuff like that – it’s just…and that really annoys – if anything, ever if I’m look down, for whatever reason, like for instance my grandpa died, last year, and I looked down and I went into the department, I thought chin up, I’ve got a deadline, chin up, go in, and my close friends knew and they were a bit – ‘cos you just don’t know how to act and it’s just like treat me blooming normally will you? You’ll make me cry. And then a lad walked past and he was like, oh is it time of the month? And you’re just like – how – what gives him the right to say that personal thing to me. Like I don’t start talking about bodily men’s stuff, you know, it’s like – I could come out with all kinds of things but I won’t do it but I wouldn’t dream of going up to somebody else and saying – like girls joke and we say it to each other, ‘cos you can tell, but the lads don’t have a clue – so, it’s gonna take a long, long, long, long, long time. And, it might happen when it – for instance like my room mate is Dutch and she seems to have a completely different outlook on almost everything in life but she’s doing international business like my mother, so she’s very vocal about politics and rights, and feminism and everything like that. Whether you like it or not, she’ll talk to you about it, and she uses this chat up line (lost words) and she started telling people about feminist rights and I was studying this today and you can see the lads going (sharp intake of breath) feminist lesbian, move out the way - but she’s lovely – she really is lovely but she’s – she doesn’t see any barrier between men and women in industry, or anything, because the world’s an open book to her and in that way I think she’s naïve but she honestly believes that if she believes in herself she can achieve anything, and I think – I agree with that to a certain extent, but there’s always going to be somewhere – a big chairman, somewhere, that got the job because his grandfather’s grandfather has always had the job. He’s gonna be a bit threatened by this woman coming into the engineering industry because – for instance, whenever I go into interviews, I have like this big issue talking about the suits – because I’ve got a trouser suit and nothing against trousers obviously, but personally I would feel – because I have to wear trousers all day, every day for my course – I would feel more comfortable in my skirt suit – only because I’ve grown taller I can’t wear it, because it’s a bit wee but it’s just – I don’t want to see – I feel I would be at a loss if I went into an interview, in a skirt, and that shouldn’t be an issue. I mean if you were a bloke and you went into an interview in a skirt, fair enough you’d be at a loss but it shouldn’t be – I shouldn’t have to dress with big kind of like power shoulder blades – shoulder pads, you know, the big power suit type job, to try and blend in, in a masculine environment. I shouldn’t have to blend in like a bloke. You know, cos I’m there in my own right and if I want my hair down, I’ll have my hair down and stuff like that. I don’t want to – I’m not gonna kick up a stink, but I don’t feel I should hide who I am. Sorry, I’ve rambled for ages.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: No, that’s OK, that’s been really interesting. Thank you very much.
